In the Sierra Madre Occidental in the state of **Chihuahua** lies the **Copper Canyon**, in Spanish **Barranca del Cobre**. It consists of several deep gorges. Together they are larger than the Grand Canyon in the USA. A famous railway runs through this area, over many bridges and through tunnels.

In the mountains and gorges of Chihuahua lives the indigenous people of the **Rarámuri**, also called the **Tarahumara**. Their name means roughly “those with the light feet”. The Rarámuri are famous for **long-distance running**. They often run very long distances in simple sandals. For them running is part of festivals and old games.

The **Sierra Madre del Sur** stretches through the states of **Guerrero** and **Oaxaca**. It drops steeply to the Pacific coast, where the city of **Acapulco** also lies. In the north-east lies the industrial city of **Monterrey** at the foot of the Sierra Madre Oriental. There the mountain **Cerro de la Silla** is well known, which means “saddle mountain”.

gewusst: The gorges of the Copper Canyon are together larger than the Grand Canyon.
In races the Rarámuri sometimes run distances longer than a marathon.

teile.einleitung: The horse latitudes are areas of weak wind on both sides of the equator, at about 30 degrees of latitude. Sailing ships used to fear them, because there for days on end hardly any wind blew.
wichtigste: The horse latitudes lie at about 30 degrees north and south latitude.
There lie the subtropical high pressure belts.
Weak winds and little precipitation are typical.
From the horse latitudes the trade winds blow towards the equator and the westerlies towards the poles.
The Azores High belongs to the high pressure belt of the northern hemisphere.
The Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic lies in the horse latitudes.
Because a lot of water evaporates and little rain falls, the sea there is especially salty.

abschnitte.text: The name **horse latitudes** is very old. A widespread explanation goes like this: sailing ships there often got into a **calm**, that is, a lack of wind. The voyage then took much longer, and drinking water and fodder ran short. That is why **horses** are said to have been thrown overboard. Whether that was really so is not quite certain. In English the areas are called “horse latitudes”.

At the equator warm air rises. At great height it flows towards the poles and sinks again at about **30 degrees of latitude**. There the **subtropical high pressure belts** form. The **sinking air** warms up, and as a result clouds dissolve. That is why it rarely rains in the horse latitudes. In this belt lie large deserts such as the **Sahara**.

In the horse latitudes themselves it is often calm. At ground level, however, the air flows out of the high pressure area. Towards the equator blow the **trade winds**, steady winds that seafarers once liked to use. Towards the poles blow the **westerlies**. These westerlies often bring Switzerland weather from the Atlantic too.

The **Azores High** over the Atlantic belongs to the high pressure belt of the northern hemisphere. It is very important for the weather in Europe. In summer the high pressure belt **shifts** to the north. That is why summers on the **Mediterranean** are mostly hot and dry. When the Azores High reaches far to the north, it brings Switzerland fine summer weather too.

In the horse latitudes of the North Atlantic lies the **Sargasso Sea**. It is known for its calm and for **drifting seaweed** that floats on the surface of the water. Because in the horse latitudes a lot of water **evaporates** and little rain falls, the **salt content** of the sea there is especially high.

gewusst: The Sargasso Sea is a sea with no coast at all; it is bounded only by ocean currents.
Many of the largest deserts on Earth lie near the horse latitudes.

teile.einleitung: Spitsbergen is a group of islands far in the north in the Arctic Ocean. It belongs to Norway and is called Svalbard in Norwegian. Here there are glaciers, polar bears and a vault in which plant seeds from all over the world are stored.
wichtigste: Since the Svalbard Treaty of 1920 Spitsbergen has belonged to Norway.
In Norwegian the group of islands is called Svalbard.
The largest settlement is Longyearbyen.
In the Global Seed Vault seeds of crop plants are kept.
Willem Barents gave the islands their name in 1596.
Because of the polar bears, you need protection outside the settlements.

abschnitte.text: Spitsbergen lies far north of the mainland of Norway, halfway to the North Pole. Large parts of the islands are covered by **glaciers**. In Norwegian the whole group of islands is called **Svalbard**, which means roughly “cool coast”. The largest island bears the name **Spitsbergen**. In summer the Sun does not set for months, and in winter the **polar night** lasts a long time.

The Dutch navigator **Willem Barents** sighted the islands in **1596**. He named them “Spitsbergen”, meaning pointed mountains, after their sharp mountain peaks. The **Barents Sea** is also named after him. For a long time several countries argued over the islands. In the **Svalbard Treaty**, signed in Paris in 1920 and in force from 1925, **Norway** received sovereignty. Citizens of the treaty states may nevertheless carry out economic activities there.

The largest settlement is **Longyearbyen**. It is the seat of administration and has about 2,500 inhabitants. It is regarded as one of the northernmost settlements of this size in the world. In the past people here lived mainly from **coal mining**. Today research and tourism are also important.

In a mountain near Longyearbyen lies the **Svalbard Global Seed Vault**. There **seed samples** of crop plants from all over the world are stored, for example of grain, rice and beans. They are a reserve in case varieties are lost through wars, natural disasters or diseases. The cold in the mountain helps to keep the seeds for a long time.

On Spitsbergen live **polar bears**. They can be dangerous for people. Anyone who leaves the settlements must therefore carry suitable **protection** or travel with an experienced guide. Reindeer, Arctic foxes, walruses and many seabirds also live here. Nature is strictly protected.

gewusst: In the Global Seed Vault on Spitsbergen there are seeds from almost all countries of the world.
On Spitsbergen the Sun does not set for weeks in summer.

teile.einleitung: A special economic zone is an area in which different economic rules apply than in the rest of the country. Firms there get, for example, lower taxes. Especially well known are the special economic zones in China, which came into being from 1980.
wichtigste: In special economic zones tax and customs advantages apply for companies.
They are meant above all to attract foreign direct investment.
China’s first four zones came into being in 1980: Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou and Xiamen.
They arose from the policy of reform and opening up under Deng Xiaoping.
In 1988 the whole province of Hainan became a special economic zone.
The zones served as a testing ground for market-economy reforms.

abschnitte.titel: What is a special economic zone?
abschnitte.text: A **special economic zone** is a defined area with special rules for the economy. Companies there receive **lower taxes**, **customs relief** on the import of intermediate goods and more freedom. In this way **foreign direct investment** is meant to be attracted. That means: foreign firms build factories, bring money and technology and create jobs. Such zones exist in many countries of the world.

After decades of a strictly state-controlled economy, **Deng Xiaoping** began the **policy of reform and opening up** from 1978. China now allowed market-economy elements and foreign investment. In 1980 the first four special economic zones came into being: **Shenzhen**, **Zhuhai**, **Shantou** and **Xiamen**. Three lie in the province of Guangdong, Xiamen in Fujian. All of them are on the south-east coast.

The places were chosen deliberately. **Shenzhen** borders directly on **Hong Kong**, **Zhuhai** on **Macau**, which was then under Portuguese administration. The closeness was meant to attract capital and knowledge from these territories. In 1988 the island of **Hainan** became a province of its own and at the same time was declared a special economic zone as a whole.

**Shenzhen** is the best-known special economic zone of China. In 1980 it was still a small border town. According to the **2020 census**, Shenzhen had about 17.6 million inhabitants. Today the city is a large centre of technology and electronics. Many well-known Chinese firms have their headquarters there.

For China the special economic zones were like a **laboratory**. The government tested new rules for the economy there. What proved its worth was later extended to other regions. In this way the zones helped China become one of the largest economic powers in the world. Critics also point, however, to great differences between rich coastal cities and poorer areas in the interior of the country.

gewusst: In about 40 years Shenzhen grew from a small border town into a megacity.
The whole island of Hainan is a single special economic zone.

teile.einleitung: Suburbanisation means that people and businesses move from the city to the suburbs and the surrounding area. In this way cities spread out into the countryside. In Switzerland and in many other countries this has greatly changed the landscape.
wichtigste: In suburbanisation homes, shops and firms move from the city to the surrounding area.
It was promoted most strongly in the 20th century by mass motorisation.
In 1970 the Shoppi opened in Spreitenbach, one of the first large shopping centres in Switzerland.
A common consequence is urban sprawl.
In 2013 the Swiss electorate accepted the revision of the Spatial Planning Act.
The Sprawl Initiative was rejected in 2019.

abschnitte.text: In the 20th century more and more families could afford a **car**. With this **mass motorisation** people could live far away from their place of work. **Cheap building land** and the wish for a **detached house** of one’s own with a garden strengthened the trend. In this way ever larger **urban areas** grew around the cities. This movement into the surrounding area is called **suburbanisation**.

abschnitte.titel: Shopping on the edge of town
abschnitte.text: Not only homes moved out, but also **retail**. In March **1970** the **Shoppi** opened in **Spreitenbach** in the canton of Aargau, one of the first large shopping centres in Switzerland. It lay at the gates of Zurich and was easy to reach by car. In the USA **Levittown** on Long Island became the symbol of the suburbs: from the late 1940s the firm Levitt & Sons built thousands of almost identical houses there in series.

The urban development model by **van den Berg** describes four phases: **urbanisation**, suburbanisation, **counterurbanisation** and **reurbanisation**. In counterurbanisation the whole urban area loses inhabitants. When the centre of a city loses inhabitants while the ring around it grows, people speak of the **doughnut effect**: as with a doughnut, a hole is left in the middle.

A common consequence of suburbanisation is **urban sprawl**. Houses, roads and commercial areas spread out into the countryside without order. This needs a lot of **land** and causes a lot of **traffic**. Meadows, fields and habitats for animals and plants are lost.

Switzerland is trying to slow down sprawl. In **2013** the electorate accepted the **revision of the Spatial Planning Act**, which came into force in 2014. It requires that oversized **building zones** be reduced and that development be **concentrated inwards**, that is, that existing settlements be used better. The **Sprawl Initiative** of the Young Greens wanted to limit building zones overall. People and cantons clearly rejected it in February **2019**.

gewusst: The Shoppi Tivoli in Spreitenbach is still one of the largest shopping centres in Switzerland.
In Levittown the houses looked so alike that the place became a symbol of the suburbs of the USA.

teile.einleitung: The Sahel is a broad belt in Africa that stretches south of the Sahara from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. Here the desert gradually turns into savannah. People’s lives depend strongly on the scarce rain.
wichtigste: The Sahel lies between the Sahara in the north and the damper savannah in the south.
Only about 100 to 600 millimetres of rain fall a year, mostly in a few summer months.
Typical plants are grasses, thorn bushes, acacias and baobabs.
In the 1970s and 1980s there were severe droughts and famines.
The Sahel states include Senegal, Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad.
The Great Green Wall is meant to slow the spread of the desert.

abschnitte.text: The name **Sahel** comes from Arabic and probably means **shore** or **coast**. For caravans that had crossed the Sahara, the Sahel was like the saving shore of a sea of sand. The belt reaches from Senegal and Mauritania in the west to Sudan and Eritrea in the east. It is a few hundred kilometres wide and several thousand kilometres long.

abschnitte.titel: Little rain, a lot of dust
abschnitte.text: In the north of the Sahel only about 100 millimetres of rain fall a year, in the south about 600 millimetres. By comparison: in Zurich it is over 1,000 millimetres. The rain comes almost only in the **rainy season** in summer, and the rest of the year is dry. In winter the **Harmattan** often blows, a dry north-east wind from the Sahara. It brings dust and cool nights as far as the Gulf of Guinea.

Many families grow **millet**, a grain that needs little water and grows on barren soils. Many herders live as **nomads**: they follow the rain and the fresh grass with cattle, goats, sheep and camels. In this way they make the best use of the scarce pastures. Trees such as acacias and the thick **baobab** provide shade, fodder and fruit.

In the 1970s and 1980s the rain stayed away for several years. Harvests failed, many animals died, and many people went hungry or had to leave their homes. When drought, **overgrazing** and deforestation come together, the soil loses its plant cover. It dries out, and areas like deserts form. This process is called **desertification**.

In 2007 the African Union launched the **Great Green Wall** project. Right across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti, a belt of trees, shrubs and greened areas is to be created. It is meant to protect the soil and help people to grow more again. The project is making good progress in some countries, in others only slowly.

gewusst: Saharan dust that the wind carries across the Sahel can fly as far as Europe and sometimes even colours the snow in the Swiss Alps yellowish.
The baobab can store a lot of water in its thick trunk and so survive long dry spells.

teile.einleitung: A savannah is a wide grassland with scattered trees. It usually lies between the rainforest and the desert. The savannahs of Africa, with lions, elephants and giraffes, are especially well known.
wichtigste: In the savannah mainly grass grows, with scattered trees.
It usually lies between rainforest and desert.
There is a rainy season and a dry season.
Large savannahs with lions are found in Africa.
Typical animals are the giraffe, zebra, elephant and cheetah.
The Serengeti in Tanzania is a famous national park.

abschnitte.titel: Grass as far as the eye can see
abschnitte.text: The **savannah** is a landscape with a lot of **grass** and only scattered trees or shrubs. The grass can grow taller than a child. Savannahs usually lie **between the rainforest and the desert**. The largest are in **Africa**, but savannahs are also found in South America, India and Australia.

The climate of the savannah has two main seasons. In the **rainy season** a lot of rain falls, the grass turns green and the animals find enough food. In the **dry season** it hardly rains for months, the grass turns yellow and many waterholes dry up. Then many animals travel long distances in search of water and grass.

A typical tree of the African savannah is the **baobab**. Its trunk is very thick and can store a lot of water. In the dry season it loses its leaves to save water. **Acacias** with flat, umbrella-shaped crowns also grow in the savannah.

The **giraffe** uses its long neck to eat leaves high up in the trees. **Zebras** are recognised by their black and white stripes. The **African elephant** is the largest land animal in the world. The **cheetah** is the fastest land animal and can briefly reach over 90 kilometres an hour. Lions, rhinoceroses, antelopes and wildebeest also live here.

A famous national park with savannah is the **Serengeti** in **Tanzania**. Every year over a million **wildebeest**, together with zebras and gazelles, travel in a great circle through the land. They follow the rain and the fresh grass. The Serengeti is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

gewusst: A cheetah can run very fast, but can keep up the speed only for a short time.
Some baobabs are over a thousand years old.

teile.einleitung: Lake Tanganyika is a huge lake in East Africa. It is the longest freshwater lake on Earth and is famous for its many colourful fish.
wichtigste: Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake on Earth, about 670 kilometres.
It borders four countries: Tanzania, Congo, Burundi and Zambia.
It lies in the East African Rift Valley.
About 250 species of cichlids live in the lake.
Water flows out towards the Congo via the River Lukuga.

abschnitte.text: Lake Tanganyika is about **670 kilometres long**, but mostly only about 50 kilometres wide. No other freshwater lake is as long. It is also very deep, the **second deepest lake** on Earth after Lake Baikal. **Four countries** lie on its shore: **Tanzania**, the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**, **Burundi** and **Zambia**. Tanzania and Congo have the largest shares.

The lake lies in the **East African Rift Valley**. There the **Earth's crust** is slowly drifting apart, and the ground sinks between steep edges. Water collected in this rift. The lake is several million years old. Water flows out to the west via the **River Lukuga** and reaches the **Congo** and finally the Atlantic.

About **250 species** of **cichlids** live in Lake Tanganyika. Most of them are found nowhere else in the world. In the very old lake they developed over a long time into many species. That is why the lake is famous among **researchers** and aquarium lovers. For the people on the shore, fishing is very important.

In 1858 the British explorers **Richard Burton** and **John Speke** were the first Europeans to reach the lake. They were looking for the sources of the Nile. In 1871 **Henry Morton Stanley** found the missing explorer **David Livingstone** in **Ujiji** on the lakeshore. He is said to have greeted him with the famous words “Dr Livingstone, I presume?”

gewusst: On the shore of the lake lies Gombe National Park, where Jane Goodall studied chimpanzees.
After Lake Baikal, Lake Tanganyika holds the most fresh water of any lake.

teile.einleitung: The sector model is a model that describes how cities are laid out. It shows the city like a cake with slices that reach outwards from the centre. The economist Homer Hoyt presented it in 1939.
wichtigste: Homer Hoyt developed the sector model in 1939.
The zones have the shape of slices of cake.
The sectors are arranged mainly along transport routes.
For this Hoyt analysed rents of homes.
All the sectors start from the business centre.
Critics complain that the model knows only one centre.

abschnitte.text: In the sector model the **business centre** lies in the middle. From there the areas radiate **wedge-shaped** outwards, like the slices of a **cake**. Each of these **sectors** has its own use, such as industry, workers’ districts or residential areas of the upper class. The sectors are arranged mainly along **transport routes**, that is, along roads, railway lines or rivers.

The economist **Homer Hoyt** published the model in **1939** in a study for the Federal Housing Administration, the US federal agency for housing loans. He studied many cities in the USA and mapped the average **rents** per block of buildings. It showed that areas with high rents had the shape of **sectors** and not of rings.

Wealthy households prefer axes with good **transport links**, a nice view or a position away from industry, often on **high ground**. The **workers’ housing area**, by contrast, lies next to the **industrial sector**, close to the factories and railway lines. In this way journeys to work are short. The upper class avoids this direction because of noise and exhaust fumes. When the city grows, a better residential area continues outwards in the **same sector**.

Hoyt built on an older model, the **concentric zone model**. In it the land uses lie in rings around the centre. The sector model extends this idea with **wedges** along the transport routes. Like the concentric zone model, however, the sector model also starts from only **one centre**. Modern cities, though, often have **several centres**. That is why other researchers later developed the **multiple nuclei model**.

A model of a city is a **simplification**. No real city looks exactly like the model. Even so, such models help to recognise patterns, for example why districts along a railway line develop in a similar way. In **geography lessons** a real city is often compared with different models, including cities in Switzerland.

gewusst: Hoyt’s model is based on data from over 140 cities in the USA.
In many cities industrial areas still lie along railway lines and rivers today.

teile.einleitung: Many countries own valuable natural resources such as oil, gas or diamonds. Surprisingly, some of these countries still do badly economically. This puzzle is called the resource curse.
wichtigste: The British economist Richard Auty coined the term “resource curse” in 1993.
In English it is also called the “Paradox of Plenty”.
“Dutch disease” weakens other industries through a strong currency.
A rentier state is financed mainly from income from raw materials instead of from taxes.
Because raw material prices fluctuate greatly, state income fluctuates too.
Norway invests its oil income abroad in a sovereign wealth fund.
The EITI initiative campaigns for transparency in the raw materials sector.

abschnitte.titel: Rich in raw materials, poor in growth
abschnitte.text: A **resource curse** exists when a country grows more slowly than other countries despite rich natural resources. The term was coined by the British economist **Richard Auty** in 1993. In English it is called the **resource curse** or also the **Paradox of Plenty**. There are various reasons for it. Not every country rich in raw materials is affected, however.

When a country sells many raw materials, a lot of foreign money flows into the country. This makes its own **currency** more valuable. Other goods from this country become more expensive abroad and sell less well. As a result **industry** and other export sectors suffer. This effect is called **Dutch disease**, because it was observed in the Netherlands after large finds of natural gas.

A state that is financed mainly from income from raw materials instead of from taxes is called a **rentier state**. Experts suspect that the government then depends less on its citizens. A further problem: **raw material prices fluctuate greatly**. If the price falls, the state suddenly lacks a lot of money. **Venezuela** has the largest oil reserves in the world and fell into a severe economic crisis after the collapse in the oil price from 2014.

**Norway** is seen as an example of how to avoid the resource curse. The country invests its oil income abroad in a large **sovereign wealth fund**. In this way the economy is not flooded with money, and the wealth is kept for later generations. **Saudi Arabia** wants to make its economy less dependent on oil with the plan **Vision 2030**. The **EITI** initiative demands transparency about payments in the raw materials sector, so that it becomes visible where the money goes.

Switzerland itself has hardly any natural resources. Even so, it is very important in the raw materials business. Many large **commodity trading firms** have their headquarters in Switzerland. **Geneva** is regarded as one of the most important trading centres for oil in the world. Switzerland also supports the **EITI** initiative.

gewusst: Botswana is seen as an example showing that income from diamonds can also lead to prosperity.
The Norwegian sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Southern Patagonian Ice Field is a huge area of ice in the Andes in the south of South America. Outside Antarctica it is the largest mass of ice in the southern hemisphere.
wichtigste: The ice field lies in the southern Andes in Patagonia.
It lies in the territory of Chile and Argentina.
It is about 350 kilometres long.
Outside Antarctica it is the largest mass of ice in the southern hemisphere.
Many large glaciers flow away from it, for example the Perito Moreno Glacier.

abschnitte.text: The Southern Patagonian Ice Field lies in the **Andes** in the south of South America, in an area called **Patagonia**. It stretches for about **350 kilometres** from north to south. Its area is bigger than the canton of Graubünden. Outside Antarctica it is the **largest mass of ice in the southern hemisphere**. Only in Antarctica and Greenland is there more ice in one piece.

abschnitte.titel: Glaciers that flow into the valley
abschnitte.text: From the ice field many large **outlet glaciers** flow away, that is, glacier tongues that reach down into valleys and lakes. The best known is the **Perito Moreno Glacier** in Argentina. From its high wall of ice large pieces keep breaking off into the water. The Upsala and Viedma Glaciers also belong to it. In Chile the **Pío XI Glacier** flows away, one of the largest glaciers in South America.

The ice field lies in the territory of **Chile** and **Argentina**. For a long time it was disputed where exactly the border runs across the ice. In 1998 the two countries agreed on most of the border, and one section is still open today. On the edge lie well-known national parks such as **Los Glaciares** in Argentina and **Torres del Paine** in Chile.

gewusst: Los Glaciares National Park has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage since 1981.
Many glaciers of the ice field are getting shorter because of global warming.

teile.einleitung: Samarkand is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia and lies in Uzbekistan. It was an important stop on the Silk Road. Its blue domes and magnificent buildings are famous all over the world.
wichtigste: Samarkand lies in Uzbekistan and is over 2,000 years old.
In the Middle Ages the city became rich through trade on the Silk Road.
In the 14th century Timur made Samarkand the capital of his empire.
The Registan is a square surrounded by three madrasas.
Timur’s grandson Ulugh Beg had a famous observatory built.
Blue tiles and domes shape the buildings of the city.

abschnitte.titel: A city on the Silk Road
abschnitte.text: Samarkand is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia. Even Alexander the Great came here; at that time the city was called **Maracanda**. Because it lay on the **Silk Road**, many caravans with silk, spices, paper and other goods passed through the city. Merchants from China, Persia and India met here. In this way Samarkand became very rich in the Middle Ages.

In the 14th century the ruler **Timur** made Samarkand the capital of his great empire. He conquered wide areas in Asia and brought craftsmen and artists from many countries to his city. They built magnificent mosques, palaces and tombs. Timur himself lies buried in the **Gur-e-Amir** mausoleum.

The **Registan** is the most famous square in Samarkand. It is surrounded on three sides by large **madrasas**. A madrasa is an Islamic college in which people used to learn religion, but also mathematics and astronomy. The buildings are decorated with tiles in many **shades of blue**, with patterns, lettering and stars. The old town is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

Timur’s grandson **Ulugh Beg** ruled Samarkand in the 15th century. He was very interested in astronomy and had a large **observatory** built. In it stood a huge measuring instrument, part of which was sunk into the ground. With it the scholars measured the positions of over a thousand stars very precisely. A part of this instrument has survived to this day.

gewusst: Samarkand is about as old as Rome.
Ulugh Beg’s star catalogue was long regarded as one of the most accurate in the world.

teile.einleitung: The tropical rainforest is divided into several layers, rather like a tower block. Each layer has different conditions of light, warmth and moisture. This is called the layered structure.
wichtigste: The rainforest consists of the ground and herb layer, the shrub layer, the canopy and single emergent giants.
The closed canopy lies at a height of about 30 to 40 metres.
Only about 1 to 2 per cent of the sunlight reaches the forest floor.
Buttress roots support the shallow-rooted trees.
Drip tips let rainwater run off the leaves quickly.
In the Amazon over 200 tree species can grow on one hectare.

abschnitte.text: At the very bottom lies the **ground and herb layer** with seedlings, ferns and herbs. Above it follows the **shrub layer** with shrubs and young trees. At about **30 to 40 metres** the **canopy** forms an almost closed roof of leaves. Above it only single, even taller trees stick out, the **emergent giants**. Each layer is a habitat of its own.

The dense canopy catches almost all the sunlight. Only about **1 to 2 per cent** of the light reaches the ground, where it is dim. Plants of the herb layer therefore often have especially **large, thin leaves**. In this way they catch as much as possible of the scarce light for **photosynthesis**. When an emergent giant falls, a **gap** appears. Suddenly a lot of light falls on the ground, and young trees grow quickly upwards until the roof closes again.

The soils of the rainforest are **poor in nutrients**, so the roots stay near the surface. Broad **buttress roots** nevertheless give the tall trees support. Many leaves have a long drawn-out tip, the **drip tip**. Through it rainwater runs off quickly. In this way the leaf dries faster and is less colonised by algae, fungi and lichens.

Some plants do not form a stable trunk of their own. **Lianas** are woody climbing plants that root in the ground and grow up trees into the canopy. The **strangler fig** does it the other way round: it germinates high up on a tree in the light and sends **aerial roots** to the ground. In time its roots enclose the trunk of the host tree. The host often dies, and a hollow fig trunk is left behind.

The rainforest is the habitat richest in species on land. In studies in the western **Amazon region**, well over **200 tree species** were counted on a single **hectare**. In a Swiss forest there are usually only a few species, such as beech, spruce, fir and maple. Many animal species also live only in one particular layer.

gewusst: On the forest floor it can be so dark that young trees stay small for years and wait for a gap in the canopy.
A strangler fig can grow so big that you can no longer recognise the original host tree at all.

teile.einleitung: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is one of the most famous towers in the world. It stands in the city of Pisa in Tuscany in Italy and leans clearly to one side. It is precisely this tilt that has made it world famous.
wichtigste: The tower stands in Pisa in Italy.
Building began in 1173 and took about 200 years.
The tower began to lean even during building.
It has eight storeys and is clad in white marble.
Today the top hangs about 4 metres to the side.
Visitors can climb to the top by a staircase of almost 300 steps.

abschnitte.text: The Leaning Tower is actually the **bell tower** of Pisa Cathedral. A free-standing bell tower is called a **campanile** in Italy. It stands together with the cathedral and the baptistery on a large square, the **Piazza dei Miracoli**, in English “Square of Miracles”. The tower has eight storeys, and the top one is the **belfry** with the bells. Since 1987 the square has been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**.

Building began in **1173**. Again and again it was interrupted for long periods, for example because of wars. The tower was finished only about **200 years** later. The many pauses had an advantage: the soft ground could settle slowly and become firmer. The whole tower is clad in pale **marble** and therefore shines white in the sun.

The tower stands on soft ground of **clay and sand**. Already after the first storeys it sank on one side and began to **lean**. The builders tried to make up for this: they built the upper storeys slightly slanted. That is why the tower is even slightly curved. Today the top stands almost **4 metres** to the side of the foot.

In the 20th century the tower leaned more and more, and people feared it might topple over. That is why it was closed to visitors from **1990**. Experts carefully removed earth from under the higher side, so that the tower **straightened up** a little. Since 2001 it has been open again. Visitors climb up a **staircase** of almost 300 steps, and because of the tilt walking feels a little strange.

The famous scientist **Galileo Galilei** was born in Pisa in 1564. He studied how objects **fall**. A well-known story says he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower. Whether this was really so, however, is **not certain**. Even so, many people still link the tower with his falling experiments.

gewusst: Many tourists have themselves photographed as if they were holding the tower up with their hands.
The tower is not only leaning but also slightly curved, because the upper storeys were built slanted.
In Pisa there are other buildings that lean slightly because of the soft ground.

teile.einleitung: Snow is frozen water that falls from the sky in the form of flakes. In Switzerland it belongs to winter, especially in the mountains. Snow is lovely for playing and skiing, but as an avalanche it can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: Snowflakes consist of tiny ice crystals.
A typical snowflake has six arms.
Snow falls when it is cold enough in the clouds and on the ground.
On high mountains snow lies for a long time, because it is colder up there.
Glaciers form from snow that turns to ice.
An avalanche is snow that suddenly slides down a slope.

abschnitte.text: High up in **cold clouds** water vapour freezes into tiny **ice crystals**. The crystals grow in six directions. That is why a typical **snowflake** has six arms. If it stays cold on the way down too, the flakes fall to the ground as **snow** instead of rain. In great cold, light, dry **powder snow** forms, which blows up in a cloud when you ski.

The higher you climb, the **colder** it gets. That is why there is often snow on high mountains, even when it is already warm in the valley. If the snow lies for many years, it is pressed together and turns to **ice**. In this way a **glacier** forms, a great stream of ice that flows very slowly down the valley. Because the Earth is getting warmer, more ice melts than is newly added. That is why many glaciers, in Switzerland too, are getting smaller.

An **avalanche** is a large mass of snow that thunders quickly down a slope. It is very dangerous. In Switzerland the **Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research** in Davos watches the situation and issues the **avalanche bulletin**. Ski tourers carry an **avalanche transceiver**. It sends signals, so that rescuers can find buried people more quickly.

Children like to build a **snowman**. For this you roll three balls of snow and put them on top of one another. Often he gets a **carrot nose**. You can also go sledging, have a snowball fight or build an **igloo**. Snow sticks together best when it is a little damp.

A single ice crystal is actually **transparent**. In snow, however, countless crystals lie jumbled together. They throw the light back in all directions, which is why snow looks **white**. Fresh snow contains a lot of **air**. That is why it muffles sounds, and a blanket of snow protects plants on the ground from severe frost.

gewusst: No two snowflakes look exactly the same.
Because fresh snow swallows sounds, it is often especially quiet outside after a snowfall.

teile.einleitung: The Opera House in Sydney is one of the best-known buildings in the world. With its white roofs that look like sails, it is the landmark of Australia.
wichtigste: The Opera House stands on the harbour of Sydney in Australia.
The Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the competition in 1957.
Building began in 1959 and took about 14 years.
Queen Elizabeth II opened the Opera House in 1973.
The roofs are covered with more than a million ceramic tiles.
Since 2007 the Opera House has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The roof is made up of several large, curved shells. Many people think of the **sails** of a ship, others of seashells. The shells are covered with small white and cream-coloured **ceramic tiles**. That is why they gleam in the sun and look slightly different depending on the light. The tiles are made so that the rain keeps them clean.

In 1957 the Dane **Jørn Utzon** won an international competition. His idea was bold, but nobody knew exactly how to build the curved roofs. Only after years was a solution found: the shells were put together from many identical parts. Because of arguments over costs and plans, Utzon left the project in 1966. Other architects finished the inside.

Building began in 1959 and was supposed to take only a few years. In the end it took about **14 years** and cost many times the planned amount. In **1973** Queen **Elizabeth II** opened the finished building. Today people agree that the great effort was worth it.

The Opera House stands on a **headland** in Sydney Harbour and is surrounded by water on three sides. Very close by, the **Sydney Harbour Bridge** spans the harbour. Because of its shape, people also call the steel arch bridge “the Coathanger”. Together, the Opera House and the bridge are one of the most famous photo subjects in Australia.

The Opera House has several halls for **opera, concerts, theatre and ballet**. Well over a thousand performances take place there every year. Many visitors also come just for a guided tour of the building. Since **2007** the Opera House has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, just as, in Switzerland, the old town of Bern is, for example.

gewusst: Jørn Utzon never visited the finished Opera House himself.
More than a million tiles cover the roofs.

teile.einleitung: A shield volcano is a volcano with very flat, broad slopes. It looks like a shield lying on the ground. Shield volcanoes form from runny lava and mostly erupt rather calmly.
wichtigste: Shield volcanoes are flat and very broad.
They consist of runny basalt lava.
Their slopes are usually only 2 to 10 degrees steep.
Their eruptions are mostly calm, with lava flows and lava fountains.
The islands of Hawaii are huge shield volcanoes.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the volcano **Skjaldbreiður** in Iceland. It means “broad shield”, because the mountain looks like a **warrior’s shield** lying on the ground. The whole type of volcano was named after it. Shield volcanoes are often much broader than they are high. Their slopes rise very gently, often only by **2 to 10 degrees**.

Shield volcanoes are built from **basalt lava**. Basalt is low in **silica** (SiO2); it contains only about 45 to 52 per cent of it. Little silica makes the magma **runny**. The lava therefore flows a long way before it solidifies. Layer upon layer, a broad, flat mountain forms. **Stratovolcanoes** such as Vesuvius are much steeper by comparison.

From runny lava the **gases** can escape easily. That is why large explosions are rare in shield volcanoes. The lava mostly flows out calmly in long **lava flows**, often with high **lava fountains**. This kind of eruption is called a **Hawaiian eruption**. When the surface of a lava flow solidifies, the molten rock beneath it flows on, well insulated. In this way **lava tubes** form, through which lava is carried many kilometres.

The best-known shield volcanoes on Earth stand on **Hawaii**. The islands are huge volcanoes that have grown upwards from the sea floor. They lie above a **hot spot** in the mantle. They include **Mauna Loa** and **Mauna Kea**. In **Iceland** too there are many shield volcanoes.

On Mars stands the largest known volcano in the whole solar system: **Olympus Mons**. It is a shield volcano and about **22 kilometres** high, measured from the mean level of the Martian surface. That is about two and a half times as high as **Mount Everest** above sea level. Because the surface on Mars does not shift, the lava could pour out at the same place for a very long time.

gewusst: Measured from the sea floor, Mauna Kea on Hawaii is higher than Mount Everest.
Through some old lava tubes you can walk on foot today.

teile.einleitung: The Sherpas are a people who live high in the Himalaya in Nepal. They are known as experienced mountaineers and helpers on expeditions to Mount Everest and other high peaks.
wichtigste: The Sherpas live mainly in the mountain valleys in the east of Nepal, for example in the Khumbu region.
The name Sherpa means “people from the east”, because their ancestors came from eastern Tibet.
Most Sherpas are Buddhists.
Their bodies are used to the thin air at great height.
Sherpas carry loads and secure routes for expeditions.
The Sherpa Kami Rita has climbed Mount Everest over 30 times (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: The Sherpas live in villages high in the mountains of **Nepal**, above all in the **Khumbu** region at the foot of Mount Everest. Their ancestors migrated in from the east of **Tibet** a few hundred years ago. That is why their name means “people from the east”. The Sherpas have a language of their own, which is related to Tibetan. In the past they lived mainly from farming, keeping yaks and trade.

Most Sherpas are **Buddhists**. In their villages there are monasteries, prayer wheels and colourful **prayer flags** fluttering in the wind. A well-known monastery is **Tengboche**, with a view of Everest. Many Sherpas regard the mountains as holy. Before an expedition they often hold a small ceremony and ask for protection.

At great height the air has less **oxygen**. Most people there quickly become tired or get a headache. Sherpas have lived high in the mountains for many generations. Their bodies therefore cope better with little oxygen. That is why they can work well at great height and carry heavy loads.

Many Sherpas work as **porters** and **mountain guides** for expeditions. They carry tents, food, oxygen bottles and equipment to the camps on the mountain. They lay ropes and ladders over crevasses in the ice. Without them many ascents would not be possible. The work is also dangerous, though, because of avalanches, ice falls and cold. Today porters of other origins are also often simply called “Sherpa”.

The best-known Sherpa is **Tenzing Norgay**. In 1953, together with the New Zealander **Edmund Hillary**, he was the first person to stand on the summit of Mount Everest. Today the Sherpa **Kami Rita** holds the record: in May 2026 he stood on the highest mountain in the world for the 32nd time. No other person has been up there so often.

gewusst: In the language of the Sherpas and Tibetans Mount Everest is called Chomolungma.
Kami Rita Sherpa has climbed Everest more often than any other person.

teile.einleitung: The Richter scale is the best-known scale for stating the strength of earthquakes. It was developed in the USA in 1935 and is named after the seismologist Charles Richter.
wichtigste: The Richter scale is named after the seismologist Charles Richter.
Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg presented it in 1935.
The value on the scale is called magnitude.
One step more means a deflection ten times greater on the seismogram.
The energy released is about 32 times as great per step.
The scale was originally calibrated for Southern California.
From about magnitude 6.5 the Richter scale becomes unreliable.

abschnitte.text: The American **seismologist** Charles Richter presented the scale in **1935** together with **Beno Gutenberg**. A seismologist is an expert on earthquakes. The two wanted to compare earthquakes in **Southern California** by their strength. For this they calibrated the scale for that region. Richter called the value the **local magnitude**.

A **seismometer** records the movements of the ground. The record is called a **seismogram**. The Richter magnitude refers to a particular instrument, the **Wood-Anderson seismometer**. The largest deflection is measured and converted to a distance of **100 km** from the **epicentre**. The epicentre is the point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus of the earthquake.

The Richter scale is a **logarithmic scale**. This means: if the magnitude rises by one whole step, the deflection on the seismogram is **ten times** as great. An earthquake of magnitude 6 therefore has a deflection ten times greater than one of magnitude 5. The **energy** released is even about **32 times** as great. The scale has no fixed upper limit.

With very strong earthquakes the Richter scale reaches its limits. From about **magnitude 6.5** the measured values hardly rise any more, even though the earthquake is stronger. Experts call this **saturation**. That is why today the **moment magnitude** is usually used for large earthquakes. In the news, people still often talk about the Richter scale all the same.

In Switzerland too the ground shakes, but mostly so weakly that you do not feel it. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich measures all the earthquakes in the country. The ground shakes most often in the **Valais**, in the Grisons and in the Basel region. The strongest known earthquake in Switzerland destroyed large parts of the city of **Basel** in **1356**.

gewusst: An earthquake of magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times as much energy as one of magnitude 5.
Very weak earthquakes can even have negative values on the Richter scale.

teile.einleitung: A safari is a journey on which you watch wild animals in their natural surroundings. Safaris in the national parks in the east and south of Africa are especially well known.
wichtigste: The word “safari” originally means “journey”.
Usually you drive through a national park in an off-road vehicle.
National parks protect animals and nature.
The “Big Five” are the lion, leopard, elephant, buffalo and rhinoceros.
In the early morning and in the evening you often see especially many animals.
You stay in the vehicle, and a ranger accompanies the guests.
Binoculars help you to see animals that are far away.

abschnitte.text: The word **safari** comes from **Swahili**, a language in East Africa. It originally simply means **“journey”**. In the past safaris were often hunting trips. Today the point is mostly to **watch** animals and photograph them. Well-known safari countries are, for example, **Kenya**, **Tanzania** and **South Africa**.

On a safari many guests want to see the **“Big Five”**, the great five. They are the **lion**, **leopard**, **elephant**, **buffalo** and **rhinoceros**. The name comes from the days of hunting: these animals were considered especially dangerous. Of course there is much more to discover, such as giraffes, zebras, hippos or cheetahs. The **leopard** is often the hardest to find, because it hides well.

Safaris mostly take place in **national parks** or protected areas. They serve above all for the **protection of animals and nature**. A very well-known national park in South Africa is **Kruger National Park**. In Tanzania lies the **Serengeti**, where every year huge herds of wildebeest and zebras migrate. The money from the guests often helps to pay for the parks.

You usually drive through the park in an **off-road vehicle**. You should always **stay in the vehicle**, because the animals are wild. A **ranger** or a guide accompanies the guests and knows the animals and their habits. In the **early morning** and in the **evening** many animals are active, because it is cooler then. With **binoculars** you can see even animals far away well.

gewusst: In the great animal migration in the Serengeti, more than a million wildebeest cross the savannah every year.
The Swahili word “safari” is known today in many languages of the world.

teile.einleitung: Sea water tastes salty because a lot of salt is dissolved in it. Salinity states how much salt there is in a given amount of water. It is not the same everywhere: some seas are almost fresh, others very salty.
wichtigste: A litre of sea water contains on average about 35 grams of salt.
The largest part of it is sodium chloride, that is, common salt.
Much of the salt comes from rock that rivers wash out and carry into the sea.
The Baltic Sea has brackish water, a mixture of fresh water and salt water.
At about 4 per cent the Red Sea is especially salty.
Salt water supports you better than fresh water, because it has a greater density.

abschnitte.titel: How much salt is in the sea?
abschnitte.text: On average a litre of sea water contains about **35 grams of salt**, which is about 3.5 per cent. The largest part is **sodium chloride**, which we know as common salt. Besides this there are further salts, for example with magnesium, calcium and potassium. The seas of the world contain so much salt that it could cover the continents with a thick layer.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the salt come from?
abschnitte.text: Over a long time rain dissolves tiny amounts of substances from the **rock**. The rivers carry these dissolved substances into the sea. When sea water evaporates, only the water rises into the air and the salt is left behind. In this way a lot of salt has built up over millions of years. Gases from volcanoes and hot springs on the sea floor also add substances to the sea water.

Into the **Baltic Sea** a lot of fresh water flows from rivers, and little evaporates. That is why it has **brackish water**, a mixture of fresh water and salt water. In the **Red Sea** it is hot and hardly rains, and a lot of water evaporates. That is why the salinity there is about 4 per cent. Far saltier still is the **Dead Sea**, a lake in which hardly any living thing can survive.

Salt water is heavier than fresh water; it is said to have a greater **density**. That is why it pushes the body upwards more strongly, and you swim more easily in the sea than in a Swiss lake. Salt water also freezes only at about minus 2 degrees. That is why seas freeze over less often than lakes.

In **salt works** on warm coasts, sea water is left to evaporate in shallow pools, and in this way **sea salt** is obtained. In dry countries drinking water is made from sea water. This is called **desalination**, and it needs a lot of energy. In Switzerland the Swiss salt works obtain their salt not from the sea but from layers of salt deep in the ground, which come from a primeval sea.

gewusst: Drinking sea water makes you even thirstier, because the body needs a lot of water to get rid of the salt again.
In the Dead Sea you can lie on your back and read a newspaper without sinking.

teile.einleitung: Every morning the Sun rises in the east and every evening it sets in the west. It looks as if the Sun were travelling across the sky. In reality, though, it is the Earth that turns.
wichtigste: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
At midday it stands in the south for us and at its highest.
It is not the Sun that moves, but the Earth that turns.
In summer the Sun rises early, in winter late.
Shortly before sunrise it gets light in the morning twilight.
A shadow always points away from the Sun.

abschnitte.text: In the morning the Sun appears in the **east** above the **horizon**. The horizon is the line where sky and earth seem to touch. During the day the Sun climbs higher. At midday it stands in the **south** for us in Switzerland, and then it is at its highest. In the evening it disappears in the **west**.

It looks as if the Sun were travelling across the sky. In reality the **Earth turns** on itself. For one whole turn it needs about 24 hours, that is, one day. The Earth turns from west to east. That is why we see the Sun first in the east. Places that lie further east see it earlier. **Zurich** lies further east than **Geneva**, so the Sun rises a few minutes earlier in Zurich.

Shortly before the Sun rises, the sky already gets light. This is called **morning twilight**. In the evening there is evening twilight. When the Sun is low, the sky often turns red and orange. This is the **evening glow**, or in the morning the morning glow. The light then has to take a long path through the air, and mainly red light is left over.

In **summer** the Sun rises for us before 6 o’clock and sets only late in the evening. The days are long. In **winter** it gets light much later, and the Sun sets already in the afternoon. The longest day is around 21 June, the shortest around 21 December. This is because the Earth’s axis is tilted.

A **shadow** always points away from the Sun. In the morning the Sun is in the east, so the shadow of a tree falls to the **west**. At midday the shadow is shortest, because the Sun is high. In the evening it points east and is long again. In the past people used a **sundial** to read the time in this way.

gewusst: Because the Earth turns, the Sun rises a few minutes earlier in Zurich than in Geneva.
In the morning and in the evening shadows are much longer than the object itself.

teile.einleitung: Ski tourism is an important source of income for many mountain villages in Switzerland. But climate change is making snow less reliable. That is why ski areas are looking for solutions such as artificial snow, snow storage and offers for the whole year.
wichtigste: According to the 100-day rule, a snow-reliable ski area needs at least 100 days with enough snow per season.
For every degree of warming the snow line rises by about 150 metres.
Switzerland has warmed by about 2.9 °C since pre-industrial times (as of 2024).
Technical snow works best in cold, dry air.
In snowfarming, snow is stored over the summer under wood chips.
Low-lying ski areas are the most at risk.

abschnitte.text: Many villages in the Alps live from **winter tourism**. Mountain railways, hotels, restaurants, ski schools and sports shops give work to many people. In Switzerland winter tourism began in the 19th century, for example in **St. Moritz** and **Davos**. Today Switzerland has many ski areas, from small village lifts to large areas with hundreds of kilometres of pistes.

Experts often use the **100-day rule**. A ski area counts as **snow-reliable** if it has enough snow on at least 100 days in seven out of ten winters. Otherwise running it is hardly worthwhile economically. With every degree of warming the **snow line** rises by about 150 metres. According to **MeteoSwiss**, Switzerland has warmed by about 2.9 °C, roughly twice as much as the global average (as of 2024).

Many ski areas make **technical snow**, often called artificial snow. Fine droplets of water are sprayed into the air, where they freeze. This works best in **cold, dry air**, because dry air cools the droplets further through evaporation. That is why people watch the so-called **wet-bulb temperature**. Snowmaking needs a lot of water and electricity, though, and costs a lot of money.

In **snowfarming**, snow is pushed together into large heaps in spring. These are covered with **wood chips** or sheets, which insulate like a blanket. In this way only part of it melts over the summer. In autumn it can be used to prepare a cross-country trail or piste early. In **Zermatt** you can even ski in summer on the **Theodul Glacier** near the Klein Matterhorn, but the area is shrinking because the glacier is melting.

The most at risk are **low-lying ski areas** in the Pre-Alps and the Jura. There it rains more and more often instead of snowing. In Switzerland several small ski areas have already been given up. Many mountain villages therefore rely on **year-round tourism**: hiking, mountain biking, culture and wellness spread the income across the whole year. This is also called four-season tourism.

gewusst: In Davos one of the first drag lifts in the world was built in 1934.
Switzerland is warming about twice as fast as the Earth on average, because land heats up faster than the seas.

teile.einleitung: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes right across Asia. In antiquity and in the Middle Ages it connected China with the Mediterranean region. Not only goods travelled on it, but also ideas and inventions.
wichtigste: The Silk Road connected China with the Mediterranean region.
It is named after Chinese silk.
Silk is made from the threads of a caterpillar.
Spices and precious stones were also traded.
Merchants spent the night in caravanserais.
The name “Silk Road” was coined by Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.

abschnitte.text: The Chinese were the first to know how to make **silk**, and they kept it **secret** for a long time. The threads come from the **caterpillar** of the **silkworm moth**. It spins itself into a **cocoon**, and silk is made from this thread. In the West the shiny cloth was very valuable. That is why the trade route later received its name.

The merchants travelled in **caravans**, long trains of people and animals. Often the **Bactrian camel** was among them, a camel with **two humps**. It copes well with heat and also with great cold. For overnight stays there were **caravanserais**. These were courtyards with walls in which merchants and animals could sleep safely. Hardly any merchant travelled the whole way; goods often changed owners on the way.

Besides silk, **spices**, **precious stones**, porcelain and horses were also traded. Potatoes, maize and tomatoes did not yet exist there at that time; they came later from **America**. Ideas also travelled on the Silk Road. The Chinese had invented **paper**. Along the trade routes knowledge of it reached Arabia and **Europe**. Religions such as **Buddhism** also spread along these routes.

The most famous traveller on the Silk Road is **Marco Polo** from **Venice**. He travelled to China over 700 years ago and stayed there for many years. After his return a **book** about his experiences appeared. It made many people in Europe curious about distant Asia.

People at the time did not yet know the name “Silk Road”. It was only the German geographer **Ferdinand von Richthofen** who used the term in **1877**. Before that there was no common name for these trade routes. Today parts of the old Silk Road are part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. China calls a large project for new trade routes and railway lines the “New Silk Road”.

gewusst: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of many routes over thousands of kilometres.
Today freight trains run on a modern route from China as far as Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Sandhills are a huge area of dunes in the US state of Nebraska. The dunes are not bare, however, but covered with grass. It is the largest area of its kind in North America.
wichtigste: The Sandhills lie in the Great Plains in the state of Nebraska.
They are the largest grass-covered dune area in North America.
The area is bigger than Switzerland.
Between the dunes there are many lakes and wetlands.
Most of the land is used as pasture for cattle.

abschnitte.text: The Sandhills cover a large part of **Nebraska** and together are bigger than Switzerland. The sand was blown in a long time ago by the **wind**. Today **prairie grasses** hold the dunes in place, so that they hardly move any more. If the grass cover is destroyed, however, the wind can blow the sand away again.

Under the Sandhills lies a part of a huge **groundwater reservoir**, the Ogallala Aquifer. The sand lets the rain seep away quickly. Between the dunes the water comes to the surface in many places. In this way there are hundreds of **lakes** and **wetlands** there, where many waterbirds rest.

The sandy soil is poorly suited to fields, but good as **pasture**. That is why mainly **cattle ranchers** live in the Sandhills, on large farms. The area is very thinly populated, and villages often lie far apart.

gewusst: Because the grass cover has largely been kept, the Sandhills are among the best preserved grasslands in the USA.

teile.einleitung: The platypus is one of the strangest animals in the world. It has a bill like a duck, a tail like a beaver and feet with webbing. Although it is a mammal, it lays eggs.
wichtigste: The platypus lives in the east of Australia and in Tasmania.
It is a mammal that lays eggs.
Its broad, soft bill looks like a duck’s bill.
It looks for its food in the water and finds its prey with its bill.
Males have a poisonous spur on their hind legs.
By day it rests in a burrow on the bank.

abschnitte.titel: An animal that seems made of parts
abschnitte.text: The platypus has a broad, flat **bill** like a duck, but it is soft and leathery. Its **tail** is broad and flat like a **beaver’s**, and it stores **fat** in it. On its feet it has **webbing**, with which it swims well. Its fur is dense and brown. When the first scientists in Europe saw a platypus, some thought it was a fake.

Almost all **mammals** give birth to live young. The platypus, however, **lays eggs**. Together with the **echidnas** it belongs to the **monotremes**, the only mammals that lay eggs. The young still drink **milk**. Because the platypus has no teats, the milk comes out of the skin on the belly, and the young lick it from the fur.

The platypus looks for its food in the **water** of streams and rivers. On the bottom it finds **small crustaceans**, **worms** and **larvae**. When diving it closes its eyes and ears. Its sensitive **bill** still senses the prey, because it can pick up fine movements and even weak electrical signals from the animals. It collects the prey in its cheeks and eats it at the surface.

Male platypuses have a **spur with poison** on their hind legs. For small animals the poison can be dangerous, and for humans a sting is **very painful**. By day the platypus rests in a **burrow**. It digs it with its claws into the **bank** of streams and lakes. It is active mainly at dusk and at night.

The platypus lives only in the **east of Australia** and on the island of **Tasmania**. There it needs clean water with banks into which it can dig. In Australia it is very well known and is under **protection**. It is even shown on the Australian **20 cent coin**.

gewusst: The platypus is one of the few mammals that are poisonous.
Young platypuses have small teeth, which they lose later.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is a star, that is, a huge, glowing ball of gas. It stands at the centre of our solar system and gives the Earth light and warmth. Without the Sun there would be no life on Earth.
wichtigste: The Sun is a star and much bigger than the Earth.
More than a million Earths would fit inside it.
It is about 150 million kilometres from the Earth.
Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach us.
All the planets circle the Sun.
Plants need sunlight to grow.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a **star**, like the many stars we see at night. It is just much closer to us. The Sun consists mainly of the gases **hydrogen** and **helium**. It is huge: more than **a million Earths** would fit inside it. On its surface it is about 5,500 degrees hot, and in its interior many millions of degrees.

In the sky the Sun looks small. That is because it is about **150 million kilometres** away from us. What is far away looks small. Light is very fast, but even so sunlight takes about **8 minutes** to reach the Earth. Important: never look straight at the Sun, not even with sunglasses. It can badly injure your eyes.

The Sun stands in the middle of our **solar system**. That is why it is called that. All the **planets** circle the Sun, the Earth too. For one trip round it the Earth needs a year. The **Moon** does not shine by itself. It is lit up by the Sun and throws its light back to us.

The Sun gives us **light** and **warmth**. Without it the Earth would be dark and ice cold. **Plants** need sunlight to make their food. Without light they turn yellow and die. Because animals and people eat plants, all life on Earth depends on the Sun.

The Sun is good for us, but too much of it harms the skin. You can get **sunburn**. That is why people protect themselves in summer with **sun cream**. A hat, a T-shirt and sunglasses help too. At midday the Sun is especially strong, and then shade is best.

gewusst: The sunlight you see now left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.

teile.einleitung: The Serengeti is a huge grassland in East Africa. It lies for the most part in Tanzania and is famous for its many wild animals. Every year huge herds move there across the wide plain.
wichtigste: The Serengeti is a wide grassland in East Africa.
The name means roughly “endless plain”.
To the west lies Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa.
In the north it borders the Masai Mara in Kenya.
Serengeti National Park has existed since 1951.
It is about a third as big as Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Serengeti is a wide, flat plain with **grass** and scattered trees. Such a landscape is called a **savannah**. The name comes from the language of the **Maasai**, a herding people in East Africa, and means roughly **“endless plain”**. To the west of the Serengeti lies **Lake Victoria**, the largest lake in Africa. The year is determined by the **rainy season** and the **dry season**.

The Serengeti is famous for the **great animal migration**. Well over a million **wildebeest**, together with **zebras** and **gazelles**, travel in a circle through the landscape. They follow the rain and the fresh grass. In doing so they migrate as far as the **Masai Mara** in Kenya, which joins the Serengeti directly in the north. On the way they have to cross rivers in which crocodiles lie in wait.

Where there are many plant-eaters, there are also many **predators**. In the Serengeti **lions**, **leopards** and **cheetahs** hunt. **Spotted hyenas** are also very numerous. They are spotted, and their calls sometimes sound like loud giggling or laughter. Hyenas hunt themselves, but also eat the leftovers of other animals.

In the south-east of the Serengeti lies the **Ngorongoro Crater**. It is a huge, old **volcanic crater**, on the floor of which very many animals live. At the edge of the Serengeti live the **Maasai** with their **herds of cattle**. They are a herding people in Tanzania and Kenya. Their cattle are very important to them.

**Serengeti National Park** was founded in **1951**. It is one of the oldest national parks in **Tanzania** and is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. The park is about **14,800 km²** in size. Switzerland measures about 41,300 km², so the park is a little more than a **third** as big. It was made known by the wildlife film-maker **Bernhard Grzimek** with his film “Serengeti Shall Not Die”.

gewusst: For the film “Serengeti Shall Not Die” Bernhard Grzimek received an Oscar.
In the great migration the wildebeest cover hundreds of kilometres every year.

teile.einleitung: Table salt, also called cooking salt, seasons our food and is important for the body. It is obtained from the sea or from old salt layers deep in the earth. In the past salt was so valuable that it was called “white gold”.
wichtigste: Sea salt forms when seawater evaporates in shallow pans.
Salt from a mine is called rock salt.
In Bex in Vaud you can visit a salt mine.
In the past meat and fish were preserved with salt.
Salt crystals have the shape of small cubes.
In winter road salt makes ice on the road melt.

abschnitte.text: Table salt consists almost entirely of **sodium chloride**. Our body needs salt in small amounts, for example for the nerves and muscles. Too much salt is unhealthy, though. Under a magnifying glass you can see that salt consists of small **crystals** in the shape of **cubes**. In Switzerland **iodine** is often added to table salt so that people get enough of this important substance.

Seawater contains a lot of dissolved salt. To obtain it, seawater is led into shallow pans, the **salt works** or salt gardens. The Sun makes the water **evaporate**, and the salt is left behind. Workers then rake it into heaps. In the **Dead Sea** the water is so salty that when you swim you float on the surface, almost like a cork.

Deep under the earth lie old **salt layers** from seas that dried up a very long time ago. The salt from them is called **rock salt**. In **Bex** in the canton of Vaud salt has been mined for centuries. Visitors can ride a small train into the **salt mine**. Today most of the salt in Switzerland is obtained by the Swiss Saltworks on the Rhine. Water is pumped into the ground, the salt dissolves, and the **brine** is brought up and evaporated.

In the past there were no fridges. Meat and fish were **preserved** by salting them. That is why salt was very important and at the same time rare and expensive. It was called **“white gold”**. There were trade routes of their own for salt, and whoever owned salt could become rich with it.

In winter salt is spread on **roads** and paths. Salt makes **ice and snow** melt even below zero degrees. This makes the road less slippery. Most of the salt in Switzerland is not eaten, but used as road salt or in industry. For plants at the roadside, though, too much salt is harmful.

gewusst: As early as 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries to add iodine to table salt.
In the Dead Sea you can lie on your back and read a newspaper.

teile.einleitung: The rainforest is built like a house with several storeys. At the very top it is bright and windy, at the very bottom dark and damp. In each layer different plants and animals live.
wichtigste: The rainforest has several layers, from the ground to the emergent giants.
The canopy is a dense layer of treetops.
Emergent giants stick up above the canopy and often grow over 50 metres tall.
On the ground it is fairly dark.
Most animals live in the canopy.
Fallen leaves rot very quickly.

abschnitte.titel: At the very top: the emergent giants
abschnitte.text: Some single trees are taller than all the others. They are called **emergent giants**. Many grow **50 to 70 metres** tall, as high as a tower block. They form the top layer. Up here it is sunny and windy. In the tallest trees of South America the **harpy eagle** builds its nest. It is one of the strongest birds of prey in the world and even hunts monkeys and sloths.

Below them the crowns of many trees grow close together. This creates a green **canopy**, like a roof over the forest. Here there is a lot of **light**, **blossoms** and **fruit**. That is why **most animals** live in the canopy: monkeys, birds, frogs and countless insects. On the branches grow **epiphytes** such as orchids. Up there they get more light than on the ground.

Under the canopy grow shrubs, palms and young trees. They are waiting for more light. On the trunks **lianas** climb upwards. These are climbing plants that hang like thick ropes from tree to tree. Many animals use them as a path.

abschnitte.titel: At the very bottom: the forest floor
abschnitte.text: On the ground it is **fairly dark**, because the treetops keep out almost all the sunlight. It is warm and damp. Fallen leaves **rot very quickly**, because fungi and small animals break them down fast. Large trees stand on broad **buttress roots** that grow away from the trunk like walls and give support, for the soil is not deep. In America **leafcutter ants** walk here in long lines.

gewusst: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves themselves: they grow a fungus on them in their nest, and live on that.
Some animals in the canopy hardly ever come down to the ground in their whole lives.

teile.einleitung: The St Lawrence River is a mighty river in the east of North America. It connects the Great Lakes with the Atlantic. For centuries it has been an important route for ships to Canada.
wichtigste: The St Lawrence River flows about 1,200 kilometres from Lake Ontario to the Gulf of St Lawrence.
On it lie the large cities of Montreal and Québec.
The explorer Jacques Cartier sailed up the river in 1535.
Thanks to the St Lawrence Seaway of 1959, ocean-going ships can sail into the Great Lakes.
In the estuary live white whales, the belugas.
At the outflow from Lake Ontario lie the Thousand Islands.

abschnitte.titel: From the lake to the sea
abschnitte.text: The St Lawrence River begins at **Lake Ontario** and flows about **1,200 kilometres** to the north-east. For a stretch it forms the border between **Canada** and the **USA**. Right at the start lie the **Thousand Islands**, a group of over a thousand small and larger islands. Towards the end the river grows ever wider and passes into a huge funnel. Finally it flows into the **Gulf of St Lawrence** on the Atlantic.

On its banks lie the large cities of **Montreal** and **Québec**. In this area most people speak **French**, because here lay the former colony of New France. The old town of Québec with its city walls is part of the UNESCO World Heritage. In winter the river partly freezes over in many places.

In 1535 the French explorer **Jacques Cartier** sailed up the river. He reached a village of the indigenous people at the place of present-day Montreal. Cartier hoped for a sea route to Asia, but rapids blocked the way on. Later the French founded the cities of Québec and Montreal on the river.

For a long time large ships could not sail as far as the Great Lakes because of rapids. In 1959 Canada and the USA opened the **St Lawrence Seaway**. With canals and **locks** the ships are raised step by step. Since then **ocean-going ships** can travel deep into the interior of the continent, for example with grain and iron ore.

In the estuary of the river lives a group of **belugas**. These are white whales that otherwise mostly live in Arctic waters. They are strictly protected. From boats you can also watch other whales there, including fin whales and blue whales.

gewusst: Belugas can make many different sounds, which is why they are also called the canaries of the sea.
The water of all five Great Lakes finally flows through the St Lawrence River into the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Southern Ocean surrounds the continent of Antarctica. It is very cold, often stormy and yet full of life, from tiny krill to the blue whale.
wichtigste: The Southern Ocean lies around Antarctica.
Its water is very cold, often close to freezing point.
The stormy Drake Passage lies between South America and Antarctica.
Krill is the most important food for many animals.
Blue whales, humpback whales, penguins and albatrosses live here.
The large icebergs consist of glacier ice.

abschnitte.text: The Southern Ocean surrounds **Antarctica** completely. Many experts set its boundary at **60 degrees south**. Around the continent flows the **Antarctic Circumpolar Current** from west to east, the mightiest ocean current on Earth. Between South America and Antarctica lies the **Drake Passage**. It is regarded as one of the stormiest seas in the world.

The water is **very cold** and often only a little above freezing point. In winter a huge part of the sea freezes over, and in summer the sea ice melts again. The large **icebergs** consist of **glacier ice**: they break off from the ice of Antarctica. Some are flat like huge tables and many kilometres long.

**Krill** are small, shrimp-like **crustaceans**. They live in huge swarms and eat tiny algae. Penguins, seals, fish and whales eat krill. Without krill there would be much less life in the Southern Ocean.

In summer many whales come into the Southern Ocean to eat krill. The **blue whale** is the **largest animal in the world**. The **humpback whale** stands out for its very long flippers. Over the sea soars the **albatross** on huge wings, which in the wandering albatross are over three metres across. It can glide for hours, almost without flapping its wings.

The **icefish** live in ice-cold water. In their blood they have a kind of **antifreeze**, special substances that prevent ice crystals from forming. Many icefish even have almost transparent blood without red pigment. The cold water contains a lot of oxygen, so they still manage.

gewusst: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current carries more water than all the rivers of the Earth together.
In summer a blue whale eats several tonnes of krill every day.

teile.einleitung: The South Seas is the name for the many islands in the southern and central Pacific. Many people think of palm trees, coral reefs and turquoise water.
wichtigste: The South Sea islands lie in the Pacific.
They are divided into Polynesia, Melanesia and Micronesia.
Polynesia means “many islands”.
An atoll is a ring-shaped coral island with a lagoon.
Tahiti belongs to France, and Tonga is a kingdom.
Low-lying island states such as Tuvalu are threatened by the rising sea level.

abschnitte.text: The South Seas consist of thousands of islands in the **Pacific**. They are divided into three large areas: **Polynesia**, **Melanesia** and **Micronesia**. The name Polynesia comes from Greek and means “**many islands**”. Some islands are states of their own, such as **Tonga**, which is still a **kingdom** today. Others belong to other countries, for example **Tahiti** belongs to **France**.

Many South Sea islands are **atolls**. An atoll is a **ring-shaped coral island** with a shallow lake in the middle, the **lagoon**. It forms when a coral reef grows around a volcanic island and the volcano slowly sinks into the sea. Other islands are high volcanic islands with mountains and rainforest. On the beaches **coconut palms** typically grow.

The small island state of **Tuvalu** consists of very **low-lying islands** that mostly rise only a few metres out of the sea. If the sea level rises because of global warming, flooding threatens. Salt water then gets into the groundwater and the fields. That is why island states around the world campaign for climate protection.

The people of the South Seas were great seafarers. With **outrigger canoes** they sailed from island to island, often hundreds of kilometres. They found their way by the stars, the waves and the flight of birds. In this way over many centuries they settled a huge part of the Pacific.

On many South Sea islands guests are given a **garland of flowers** to wear as a welcome. In Hawaii it is called a lei. Music, dance and shared meals are important. The painter Paul Gauguin lived on Tahiti and painted many well-known pictures there.

gewusst: In Tonga a king of its own still reigns today.
The seafarers of the South Seas found their way entirely without a compass.

t1vsefmc.t: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

teile.einleitung: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea is an international treaty about the seas. It regulates which areas of the sea belong to a state and who may fish or mine raw materials there. It is also called the “constitution of the oceans”.
wichtigste: The Convention was signed in 1982 in Montego Bay in Jamaica.
It came into force in 1994.
