A state’s territorial sea extends at most 12 nautical miles.
The contiguous zone extends to 24 nautical miles.
The exclusive economic zone extends to 200 nautical miles.
The deep seabed counts as the “common heritage of mankind”.
A nautical mile is 1,852 metres long.

abschnitte.text: The Convention was opened for signature on **10 December 1982** in **Montego Bay** in Jamaica. That is why it is also called the **Montego Bay Convention**. It came into force on **16 November 1994**, a year after the 60th ratification. Ratification means that a state officially declares the treaty valid for itself. **Switzerland** is a party to the treaty, while the **USA** have not ratified the Convention.

Measurement is made from the **baseline**, usually the coastline at low tide. A **nautical mile** is **1,852 metres** long, corresponding roughly to one minute of arc along a meridian. The **territorial sea** extends at most **12 nautical miles** (about 22 kilometres) and belongs to the state’s territory. Even so, ships of all states have the **right of innocent passage** there. Behind it lies the **contiguous zone** up to 24 nautical miles. There the state may still enforce customs, tax, immigration and health regulations.

The **exclusive economic zone**, EEZ for short, extends to **200 nautical miles** (about 370 kilometres) from the baseline. In it only the coastal state may **catch fish**, mine **natural resources** and generate energy, for example with wind farms. **Shipping** remains free for everyone there, though. Beyond it begins the **high seas**, which belong to no state.

The sea floor beyond the national areas counts as the **common heritage of mankind**. Its resources belong to no single state. It is administered by the **International Seabed Authority**, based in Kingston in Jamaica. It grants licences for the exploration and mining of raw materials, for example of **manganese nodules**. The proceeds are meant to benefit everyone.

The Convention also regulates how states can settle **disputes** over the sea. For this there is the **International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea**, based in Hamburg. **Landlocked states** such as Switzerland also have rights: they may send ships onto the high seas and have a right of access to the sea through neighbouring countries.

gewusst: Through the Convention many states received huge areas of sea, island states often far more sea than land.
The nautical mile is still the measure for distances in shipping and aviation today.

teile.einleitung: A stratovolcano is a steep, cone-shaped volcano. It is built up of many layers of lava and ash that have been laid one on top of another in many eruptions. Stratovolcanoes are among the most dangerous volcanoes on Earth.
wichtigste: A stratovolcano consists of alternating layers of lava and ash.
It usually has the shape of a steep cone.
Another word for it is composite volcano.
Stratovolcanoes often erupt explosively, because the thick lava traps gases.
They often form where one tectonic plate dives beneath another.
Mudflows of ash and water are called lahars.

abschnitte.text: With every eruption new material is laid on the mountain: once **lava**, once **ash** and lumps of rock. In this way the volcano grows upwards layer by layer. Hence the name **stratovolcano**, also called a **composite volcano**. The lava is thick and does not flow far, so a **steep cone** forms. Well-known examples are Fuji in Japan, Vesuvius in Italy and Stromboli.

Many stratovolcanoes lie at **subduction zones**. There an oceanic plate dives beneath another plate. The plate that is diving brings **water** down with it. This water **lowers the melting point** of the rock in the mantle, which therefore partly melts. The magma rises and often forms the rock **andesite**, which is named after the Andes in South America.

The thick lava traps a lot of **gas**, like a shaken bottle of fizzy drink. When the pressure becomes too great, the volcano explodes. The most violent common type of eruption is called a **Plinian eruption**. It is named after **Pliny the Younger**, who described the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 in detail. In it a huge column of ash and gas rises many kilometres high.

**Stromboli** lies on a small island north of Sicily. It is almost constantly active and throws out small fountains of glowing lava every few minutes. Sailors saw the glow at night from far away. That is why it is called the **lighthouse of the Mediterranean**.

A **lahar** is a mudflow of ash, rubble and water. It forms when rain or melted glacier snow carries away loose ash. Lahars flow fast through valleys and can bury whole towns. In 1985 an eruption of **Nevado del Ruiz** in Colombia melted parts of the glacier. Lahars destroyed the town of **Armero**, and very many people lost their lives.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are no active volcanoes, but in the nearby Hegau near Schaffhausen there are mountains that were volcanoes millions of years ago.
After the disaster at Armero, warning systems for lahars were improved in many countries.

teile.einleitung: Singapore is a small city-state in South-East Asia at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Although the country is smaller than the canton of Zurich, it is one of the most important centres of trade and finance in the world.
wichtigste: The name Singapore means “lion city”.
In 1819 Stamford Raffles founded a British trading post here.
Since 1965 Singapore has been an independent state.
Singapore has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil.
The landmark is the Merlion, a mythical creature made of a lion and a fish.
The port is one of the largest container ports in the world.

abschnitte.text: The name **Singapore** comes from **Sanskrit**, an old language of India. “Singa” means lion and “Pura” means city. The landmark is the **Merlion**, a mythical creature with a lion’s head and a fish’s body. The fish’s body is a reminder that Singapore used to be a fishing village. A large Merlion statue spouts water into the sea at the harbour.

In 1819 the Briton **Stamford Raffles** founded a **trading post** for the British East India Company. From it the modern Singapore grew. For a long time it was a British colony. In 1963 Singapore became part of the federation of **Malaysia**. After political conflicts it left again in 1965 and became an **independent city-state**. To this day many places bear the name Raffles.

In Singapore people of Chinese, Malay and Indian origin live together. That is why there are **four official languages**: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil. At about 730 square kilometres Singapore is smaller than the canton of Zurich, with about 1,700. Even so, about six million people live there (as of 2024). Many live in tall apartment blocks.

Singapore lies on one of the most important **sea routes** in the world, between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Its **port** is one of the busiest container ports on Earth. Changi **airport** is world famous too. In the **Jewel** building a huge waterfall plunges down in the middle of the interior.

Singapore likes to call itself a “city in a garden”. In the park **Gardens by the Bay** stand the **Supertrees**. These are artificial trees of steel up to 50 metres high, covered with plants. In the evening they light up in a light and music show. The climate is warm and humid all year round, because Singapore lies close to the equator.

gewusst: In Changi airport a waterfall several storeys high plunges down inside the building.
Singapore is one of the few city-states in the world.

teile.einleitung: Saint-Martin is a small island in the Caribbean. The special thing is that it belongs to two countries at the same time. The north is French, the south belongs to the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
wichtigste: Saint-Martin lies in the Caribbean, in the Lesser Antilles.
France and the Netherlands share the island.
The French part is called Saint-Martin, the Dutch part Sint Maarten.
The island is only just under 90 square kilometres in size.
Tourism is the most important source of income.

abschnitte.text: Saint-Martin is one of the smallest inhabited islands in the world that two states share. The northern part belongs to **France**, and the southern part is called **Sint Maarten** and is a country of its own within the **Kingdom of the Netherlands**. The division goes back to a treaty of 1648. There is hardly any guarded border, and you can simply drive across.

The island lives mainly from **tourism**. Visitors come for the beaches, the warm sea and the cruise ships. Famous is **Maho Beach** in the Dutch part: the aeroplanes land there so low over the bathers that many people come especially to watch. In the French part people pay with the euro.
Saint-Martin lies in an area where **hurricanes** often form in late summer and autumn. In 2017 Hurricane **Irma** destroyed a large part of the houses and roads. The rebuilding took several years.

gewusst: Saint-Martin is about as big as Lake Zurich, and yet two countries share the island.

teile.einleitung: Why does a firm build its factory in one particular place? That depends on the location factors. These are all the features of a place that matter to a business.
wichtigste: Location factors determine where businesses settle.
Hard location factors can be measured and expressed in costs.
Soft location factors are harder to measure, such as quality of life or the reputation of a region.
Regions compete as locations for firms and jobs.
Low corporate taxes are one reason why the canton of Zug attracts many company headquarters.
Because transport became cheaper, transport costs have become less important for many industries.

abschnitte.text: **Hard location factors** can be recorded in numbers. They include, for example, **land prices**, **taxes**, wages, energy prices and **transport links**. The availability of **skilled workers** can also be measured. A business can include these factors directly in its cost calculation. The canton of **Zug**, for example, has low tax rates for firms by Swiss comparison.

**Soft location factors** are harder to put into numbers. Two kinds are often distinguished. **Business-related** soft factors concern, for example, the economic climate or the reputation of a region. **Person-related** soft factors concern the quality of life of the employees, such as housing, schools, culture and leisure. For highly qualified experts, who can often choose where they work, these factors are becoming more and more important.

Depending on the industry, different factors come first. A **market-oriented** business such as a bakery or a shop needs to be close to its customers. **Energy-oriented** were, for example, the early **aluminium smelters**: they need a great deal of electricity and therefore arose where cheap **hydropower** was available, for example in **Valais**. Other businesses go by raw materials or by labour.

Often similar businesses settle close to one another. Then **contact advantages** arise: the firms can easily make contacts, exchange knowledge and give one another orders. Suppliers and specialised skilled workers are then also nearby. An example in Switzerland is the watch industry in the Jura.

States, cantons and communes try to attract firms with taxes, good infrastructure and quality of life. This is called **location competition**. The importance of the factors changes over time. Since the 20th century transport has become much cheaper and faster thanks to **container ships**, motorways and air freight. That is why today labour, taxes and quality of life often play a bigger role than transport costs.

gewusst: As early as 1909 the German economist Alfred Weber wrote a well-known theory about where industrial businesses settle.
Making aluminium needs so much electricity that aluminium is sometimes called “packaged electricity”.

teile.einleitung: Stratus is a low, grey cloud that covers the sky like an even blanket. The word comes from Latin and means “spread out”. In Switzerland this cloud is known mainly as high fog.
wichtigste: Stratus is a low, grey layer cloud.
The name means “spread out”.
Stratus can bring light drizzle.
When the cloud lies on the ground, it is called fog.
On the Swiss Plateau high fog often forms in autumn and winter.

abschnitte.text: **Stratus** is one of the **low clouds**. It often lies only a few hundred metres above the ground. Unlike the puffy heap clouds, it has no clear shapes. It is an even, grey **layer cloud** that can cover the whole sky. The Sun can then be seen only as a pale disc or not at all. From stratus at most light **drizzle** or a little snow falls, but no heavy rain.

When the stratus layer lies directly on the ground, it is called **fog**. When it lifts a little off the ground, people speak of **high fog**. In autumn and winter a blanket of high fog often lies over the Swiss **Plateau** for days. Cold air collects below, and warmer air lies above it, like a lid. This is called an **inversion**.

Anyone who climbs a mountain in high fog, for example the Rigi, the Pilatus or in the Jura, often experiences something wonderful. Above the layer of cloud the Sun shines, and below lies a white **sea of fog**. Only the mountain peaks stick out like islands. For the people in the valley, by contrast, it stays grey and cool.

gewusst: Stratus is one of the lowest clouds of all, and sometimes it even touches hills and tall buildings.
In high fog it can be clearly warmer and sunnier on a mountain than down in the valley.

teile.einleitung: City tourism means that people travel to a city to visit it. They look at museums and sights, go to concerts or travel for their work. Cities profit from it, but sometimes also have too many guests.
wichtigste: City trips are mostly short and often last only one to three nights.
From the 1990s low-cost airlines promoted short trips to European cities.
MICE stands for Meetings, Incentives, Conventions and Exhibitions.
Zurich has the most hotel overnight stays in Switzerland.
In many Swiss communes guests pay a tourist tax.
The Louvre in Paris is regarded as the most visited museum in the world.

abschnitte.text: City trips mostly last only **one to three nights**. Many people visit a city such as London, Barcelona or Berlin at the weekend. From the 1990s the growth of **low-cost airlines** strongly promoted such short trips, because cheap flights made them affordable for many. Popular destinations are museums, old towns, shopping streets and events.

Not all guests travel on holiday. An important part is business and conference tourism. It is called **MICE**: this stands for **Meetings**, **Incentives** (reward trips for employees), **Conventions** (congresses) and **Exhibitions** (trade fairs). It brings cities such as **Zurich**, **Geneva** or **Basel** many overnight stays during the week. In the statistics of the Federal Statistical Office, Zurich is regularly ahead of Geneva and Basel.

Culture is a magnet for many cities. The **Louvre** in Paris is regarded as the most visited museum in the world, and the biggest draw is the **Mona Lisa**. Since **1985** a **European Capital of Culture** has been named every year, the first being **Athens**. The idea came from the Greek minister of culture Melina Mercouri. The title often brings cities more visitors.

In many Swiss communes guests pay a **tourist tax** per overnight stay. With it the communes finance services for guests, such as guest cards or events. In other cities such a charge is called a **city tax**. Overnight statistics do not show the whole of tourism, though: **day visitors** such as cruise passengers or excursionists are not counted, even though they also use the city.

abschnitte.titel: When there get to be too many
abschnitte.text: When very many guests come, people speak of **overtourism**. Lanes are overcrowded, flats are turned into holiday flats, and the residents feel disturbed. **Amsterdam** therefore decided in 2024 to approve no new hotels, unless another one closes. The city wants to limit overnight stays to **20 million** a year. Other cities too are looking for ways to steer tourism better.

gewusst: Day visitors do not appear in any hotel statistics, even though in some cities they make up a large part of the visitors.
The Louvre counts roughly eight to nine million visits a year.

teile.einleitung: Seoul is the capital of South Korea and one of the largest cities in Asia. The River Han flows right through the city. Seoul combines old royal palaces with modern tower blocks.
wichtigste: Seoul is the capital of South Korea.
The Han flows through Seoul.
In 1988 the Summer Olympic Games took place in Seoul.
The largest royal palace is Gyeongbokgung.
About half of South Koreans live in the Seoul metropolitan area.

abschnitte.text: The River **Han** divides Seoul into a northern and a southern part. **More than 25 bridges** cross it. Along the bank there are long parks in which people walk, cycle and picnic. Around the city lie wooded **mountains**. Seoul has been the capital of Korea since the 14th century.

The largest royal palace in Seoul is **Gyeongbokgung**. It was built in **1395** for the kings of the **Joseon dynasty**. This ruling family governed Korea for over 500 years. Today the palace is one of the best-known destinations in the city. Many visitors rent a **hanbok** there, a traditional Korean garment.

In **1988** Seoul was host of the **Summer Olympic Games**. They were only the second Summer Games in Asia, after **Tokyo 1964**. The Games made the city and South Korea better known worldwide. For the Games many new sports facilities and roads were built.

In the **Seoul metropolitan area**, with the city of **Incheon** and the province of **Gyeonggi**, live about **26 million** of the roughly 51 million South Koreans (as of 2023). That is about **half** of the country’s population. Seoul is the centre of economy, politics and culture. Many large firms have their headquarters here, and the city has a very dense **metro network**.

gewusst: The Korean script Hangul was created in the 15th century under a king of the Joseon dynasty.
Only about 50 kilometres north of Seoul runs the border with North Korea.

teile.einleitung: Saudi Arabia is a large country on the Arabian Peninsula. A large part of it is desert. Oil has made the country rich, and in Mecca lies the holiest city of Islam.
wichtigste: The capital of Saudi Arabia is Riyadh.
The country lies on the Arabian Peninsula and is about 50 times bigger than Switzerland.
Mecca is the holiest city of Islam.
Oil has made Saudi Arabia rich.
There is no river that carries water all year round.
People speak Arabic and pay with the riyal.

abschnitte.text: Saudi Arabia covers the largest part of the **Arabian Peninsula**. It is about **50 times bigger than Switzerland**. In the west it borders the **Red Sea**, in the east the **Persian Gulf**. In the south lies the **Rub al Khali**, the largest continuous sand desert in the world. There is **no river** that carries water all year round, only dry valleys that briefly have water after rare rain.

In **Mecca** stands the **Kaaba**, the most important sanctuary of Islam. Here the Prophet Muhammad was born. Every year millions of Muslims come to Mecca for the pilgrimage called the **Hajj**. **Medina**, where Muhammad is buried, is also a holy city. Muslims all over the world turn towards Mecca when they pray.

In 1938 large **oil deposits** were discovered in Saudi Arabia. Today the country is one of the largest oil producers in the world. With the money, cities, roads, airports and schools were built. Because the oil will not last for ever, the country is trying to strengthen other areas too, such as tourism.

Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932 by **Ibn Saud** and named after his family. The country is a **monarchy**, with a king at its head. There is no elected parliament as in Switzerland. The national language is **Arabic**, the currency is called the **riyal**. The capital **Riyadh** lies in the middle of the country and is the largest city.

gewusst: Because there is hardly any fresh water, Saudi Arabia obtains a lot of drinking water from sea water.
In Saudi Arabia there are not only deserts but also mountains, on which snow sometimes falls in winter.

teile.einleitung: The subtropics are a climate zone of the Earth. They lie between the hot tropics and the temperate zone, in which Switzerland also lies. They include, for example, the Mediterranean and large deserts such as the Sahara.
wichtigste: The subtropics lie between the tropics and the temperate zone.
On the Mediterranean the summers are hot and dry.
The winters on the Mediterranean are mild and rather wet.
Typical plants are olive trees and orange trees.
The Sahara is a large desert in the subtropics.
In the subtropics there are very many sunny days.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is divided into **climate zones**. Around the equator lie the **tropics**. To the north and south of them are the **subtropics**. After them follows the **temperate zone**, in which Switzerland also lies. In the subtropics it is warmer than with us, and the sky is very often **sunny and clear**. That is why many people travel there on holiday.

The **Mediterranean** lies in the subtropics. In **summer** it is **hot and dry** there for a long time, and it hardly rains. The **winters** are **mild**, and in this season most of the rain falls. **Olive trees** like this climate especially, which is why they grow all around the Mediterranean. **Oranges** also thrive. Many oranges that Switzerland gets in winter come from **Spain**.

Not everywhere in the subtropics does it rain in winter. There also lie large **deserts** such as the **Sahara** in North Africa. There it almost never rains. The **dromedary** is adapted to the hot desert: it has one hump and can manage for a long time without water. In hot dry areas **cacti** also grow. They store water in their thick stem, and their spines protect them from animals.

Why is it so dry and sunny in the subtropics? Here a lot of air sinks from great height. Sinking air warms up and dissolves clouds. That is why rain clouds rarely form. The areas on the edge of the subtropics, such as the Mediterranean, still get rain in winter, because then low-pressure areas pass by from the Atlantic.

gewusst: The Sahara is the largest dry desert on Earth and almost as big as the USA.
An olive tree can live for many hundreds of years.

teile.einleitung: Sublimation is the name for the change of a substance directly from the solid to the gaseous state. The liquid state is skipped. In this way snow can disappear without melting.
wichtigste: In sublimation a substance goes directly from the solid to the gaseous state.
Ice and snow can turn directly into water vapour.
This happens mainly in dry, sunny air and wind.
The reverse process is called deposition, and it is how hoar frost forms, for example.
Dry ice made of frozen carbon dioxide sublimates at normal pressure.

abschnitte.text: Normally ice first melts into water before it evaporates. In **sublimation**, by contrast, a substance goes directly from the **solid** to the **gaseous** state. Snow can in this way slowly disappear in cold but **dry** and **sunny** air without puddles forming. In the mountains this often happens, especially in wind. Frozen washing also dries on the line in winter, because the ice sublimates.

The reverse process is possible too: water vapour turns directly into ice. This is called **deposition**. This is how **hoar frost** forms on grasses and twigs on cold mornings. The **frost flowers** on cold window panes and the **snowflakes** in the clouds also form in this way. They grow directly from the water vapour in the air.

A well-known example is **dry ice**. This is frozen **carbon dioxide**. At normal air pressure it never becomes liquid, but sublimates directly into gas. In doing so a white mist forms, which is used as an effect on stages. Dry ice is very cold and must never be touched with bare hands.

gewusst: Glaciers and snowfields also lose part of their ice through sublimation.
Mothballs get smaller and smaller with time, because the substance they are made of turns directly into gas.

teile.einleitung: Shenzhen is a huge city in the south of China, right on the border with Hong Kong. About 45 years ago it was still a small place; today it is a megacity and a worldwide centre of electronics and technology.
wichtigste: Shenzhen lies in Guangdong province and borders Hong Kong in the south.
In 1980 Shenzhen became one of the first special economic zones of China.
The city belongs to the Pearl River Delta, one of the largest urban and industrial areas in the world.
In the 2020 census Shenzhen had about 17.5 million inhabitants.
The Huaqiangbei electronics market is famous for components and prototypes.
Since 2017 all city buses in Shenzhen have been electric.
Firms such as Huawei, Tencent and BYD have their headquarters in Shenzhen.

abschnitte.text: Shenzhen lies in the south of China in **Guangdong** province. In the south the city borders **Hong Kong** directly. Together with Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau, Shenzhen belongs to the **Pearl River Delta**, which is today also called the “Greater Bay Area”. In this area many millions of people live, and countless factories make goods for the whole world.

Around 1980 only a few hundred thousand people lived in the area of Shenzhen. Then the Chinese government made the place a **special economic zone**. This is an area with special rules in which foreign firms could build factories more easily. The closeness to Hong Kong brought money and knowledge to the city. In the **2020 census** Shenzhen already counted about 17.5 million inhabitants.

Shenzhen is one of the most important centres of **electronics** in the world. In the district of **Huaqiangbei** thousands of traders sell chips, screens, cables and other components. Inventors and young firms from all over the world come here to build a **prototype** quickly, that is, a first sample of a new device. Many mobile phones and computer parts are made in the region.

The technology group **Huawei** was founded in Shenzhen in 1987 and still has its headquarters there today. The internet group **Tencent** also comes from Shenzhen; it runs, among other things, the app WeChat. The carmaker **BYD** builds mainly electric cars and batteries. These firms have made the city known worldwide.

In 2017 Shenzhen became the first large city in the world to switch its whole **bus fleet** to electric drive. That was over 16,000 city buses. Many taxis also run on electricity. In this way the air in the city is getting cleaner and the streets are quieter. In addition there is a large network of metro lines.

gewusst: In only about 40 years Shenzhen grew from a few hundred thousand to over 17 million inhabitants.
Over 16,000 electric buses run in Shenzhen, more than in many whole countries.

teile.einleitung: Sajama is a mighty volcano in the west of Bolivia. At about 6,540 metres it is the highest mountain in the country. It rises at the edge of the Altiplano plateau, near the border with Chile.
wichtigste: At about 6,540 metres, Sajama is the highest mountain in Bolivia.
It is an extinct volcano with a dome of snow and ice.
It lies on the western edge of the Altiplano, near the border with Chile.
Around the mountain lies Sajama National Park, the oldest national park in Bolivia.
On its slopes trees grow at a very great height.

abschnitte.text: Sajama is a **stratovolcano** that has not erupted for a very long time. Its summit is covered with snow and ice and can be seen far across the flat plateau. The **Altiplano**, on which it stands, itself already lies about 4,000 metres above sea level. Close by, right at the border with Chile, stand more high volcanoes.

Around the mountain lies **Sajama National Park**, which was founded as the first national park of Bolivia. There small, gnarled **queñua trees** grow. They are among the trees that grow highest in the world, up to over 4,500 metres. In the park there also live **vicuñas**, wild relatives of the llama, and there are hot springs.

Sajama is a popular goal for **mountaineers**. The thin air makes the climb very tiring, though. Anyone who wants to go up must first get used to the altitude for several days. By comparison: Sajama is about 1,900 metres higher than the Dufourspitze, the highest mountain in Switzerland.

gewusst: Vicuñas have one of the finest wools in the world.
After Tibet, the Altiplano is the second largest plateau in the world.

teile.einleitung: Maritime transport is the carriage of goods and people by ship across the sea. It is the most important means of transport in world trade. Without ships many goods would not be in our shops.
wichtigste: Over 80 per cent of traded goods (by volume) travel by ship.
For large quantities ships are the cheapest means of transport.
Many goods travel in standardised containers.
The Suez Canal and the Panama Canal save ships great detours.
Switzerland too is connected to maritime transport via the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: According to the UN trade organisation **UNCTAD**, **over 80 per cent** of traded goods, measured by volume, are transported across the sea. For large quantities ships are the **cheapest** means of transport. A single ship can load as much as thousands of lorries. That is why clothes, toys, electronics, oil and grain often come to us by ship from distant countries.

For different goods there are different ships. **Container ships** carry standardised steel boxes, the **containers**. **Tankers** bring oil or gas. **Bulk carriers** load loose goods such as ore, coal or grain. There are also ships just for **cars**. For people there are **ferries** and cruise ships.

Ships sail on fixed **routes**. Artificial canals save great detours. The **Suez Canal** in Egypt connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea. In this way ships from Asia to Europe do not have to sail round the whole of Africa. The **Panama Canal** connects the Atlantic with the Pacific. If such a route is blocked, it can disrupt world trade severely.

Switzerland too depends on maritime transport. Many goods come through the large ports on the North Sea, such as **Rotterdam**. From there **Rhine ships** bring goods as far as the **Rhine ports** in Basel. In addition, since 1941 ocean-going ships have sailed the seas under the **Swiss flag**.

gewusst: The largest container ships are almost 400 metres long, longer than three football pitches end to end.
Per tonne carried, ships need far less fuel than lorries or aeroplanes.

teile.einleitung: The Seven Summits are the highest mountains of the seven continents. Climbing all seven is a great goal for many mountaineers.
wichtigste: The Seven Summits are the highest peaks of the seven continents.
The highest is Mount Everest in Asia.
Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.
Elbrus in the Caucasus is usually counted as the highest mountain in Europe.
For Australia and Oceania there are two different lists.
In 1985 Dick Bass was the first to climb all seven peaks.

abschnitte.text: The Seven Summits include the highest mountain of each continent. In **Asia** that is **Mount Everest**, the highest mountain on Earth. In **South America** it is **Aconcagua** in Argentina, in **North America** **Denali** in Alaska. In **Africa** stands **Kilimanjaro** in Tanzania. With its summit Kibo it is about **5,895 metres** high.

As the highest mountain of **Europe**, most lists give **Elbrus** in the **Caucasus** in Russia. It is about **5,642 metres** high. Because the Caucasus is usually counted as part of Europe, it is on the list. If the Caucasus were not counted as part of Europe, **Mont Blanc** on the border between France and Italy would be the highest peak.

The highest mountain of **Antarctica** is **Mount Vinson**, at about **4,892 metres**. It lies in the Ellsworth Mountains and is very remote and icy cold. For **Australia** there are two lists. The list of **Dick Bass** takes **Mount Kosciuszko** (2,228 metres) on the Australian mainland. The list of **Reinhold Messner** counts Oceania too and takes the **Carstensz Pyramid** (4,884 metres) on the island of New Guinea.

abschnitte.titel: The first on all the peaks
abschnitte.text: The American **Dick Bass** was the first to climb all the Seven Summits according to his list. He completed the series on **30 April 1985**, and the “Bass list” is named after him. The Japanese woman **Junko Tabei** stood on all seven peaks in **1992**, the first woman to do so. She was also the first woman on **Mount Everest**, in **1975**.

gewusst: Kilimanjaro can be climbed on foot without climbing equipment, yet the altitude is still a great challenge.
Mount Vinson was first climbed only in 1966.

teile.einleitung: The Salar de Atacama is the largest salt flat in Chile. It lies in the Atacama, one of the driest deserts on Earth. Beneath its salt crust lies salty water from which lithium is obtained.
wichtigste: The Salar de Atacama lies in the north of Chile at a height of about 2,300 metres.
It is the largest salt flat in Chile.
Lithium, a raw material for batteries, is obtained from its brine.
Flamingos live in its lagoons.
Lithium mining needs a lot of water and is therefore controversial.

abschnitte.titel: A salt surface in the desert
abschnitte.text: A **salt flat** forms when water evaporates in a hollow with no outflow and the salt is left behind. The Salar de Atacama lies between the Andes and a lower mountain range. Its surface is rough and crusty, not as smooth as at the Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia. Nearby lies the town of **San Pedro de Atacama**, from which many tourists visit the area.

Beneath the salt crust lies a **brine**, that is, very salty water. It contains a lot of **lithium**, a light metal that is needed for batteries in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars. The brine is pumped into large pools, where the sun makes the water evaporate. What is left behind is a solution with a lot of lithium. Chile is one of the largest lithium producers in the world.

In the lagoons at the edge of the salt flat live three species of **flamingos**. Part of the area is therefore protected as a nature reserve. Because a lot of water evaporates during mining, conservationists and the local communities worry about the scarce water. The firms and the state are looking for ways to make the mining gentler.

gewusst: In some parts of the Atacama hardly any rain was measured for years.
Flamingos are pink because they eat small crustaceans and algae with red pigments.

teile.einleitung: The Rust Belt is a region in the USA that used to live from big factories and steelworks. When many of them closed, rusting plants were left behind, hence the name.
wichtigste: “Rust Belt” literally means “belt of rust”.
It lies in the north-east and the Midwest of the USA.
Detroit is regarded as the centre of the US car industry.
From the 1970s a steep decline of industry set in.
Many jobs and people moved away to the Sun Belt in the south.
In 2013 Detroit declared bankruptcy, the largest bankruptcy of a US city up to then.
Pittsburgh is regarded as an example of successful structural change.

abschnitte.text: The **Rust Belt** lies in the **north-east** and the **Midwest** of the USA, above all around the **Great Lakes**. Across the lakes **ore and coal** could be transported cheaply by ship. That is why many steelworks and factories settled there. For a long time the region was the heart of American **heavy industry**. It used to be called the Manufacturing Belt as well, that is, the belt of factories.

**Detroit** in the state of Michigan is regarded as the centre of the **US car industry**. Large car firms had their plants there. When industry shrank, many people lost their jobs and moved away. The city took in less tax and had big debts. In **2013** Detroit declared **bankruptcy**. It was the largest bankruptcy of a city in the USA up to then.

From the **1970s** a steep **decline** set in. One important reason was **competition from abroad**, for example from **Japan**, where cars and steel were made more cheaply. In addition, machines replaced many jobs. Many firms and people moved to the warmer **Sun Belt** in the south of the USA. What was left behind was empty factories that slowly **rusted** away.

**Pittsburgh** used to be known as the **“Steel City”**. Here, too, many steelworks closed. The city then focused on **universities**, hospitals and new technology. Today it is regarded as an example of successful **structural change**. A similar example in Europe is the **Ruhr region** in Germany, which was likewise shaped by coal and steel.

gewusst: The name “Rust Belt” arose only when many factories already stood empty.
Because of its rivers and hills, Pittsburgh has several hundred bridges.

teile.einleitung: The Strait of Messina is a strait in the south of Italy. It separates the island of Sicily from the Italian mainland and connects the Tyrrhenian Sea with the Ionian Sea.
wichtigste: The Strait of Messina separates Sicily from the mainland.
At its narrowest point it is only a good 3 kilometres wide.
On one side lies Messina in Sicily, on the other the region of Calabria.
Ferries connect Sicily with Calabria.
A bridge over the strait has been planned for decades.

abschnitte.text: The **Strait of Messina** lies between the island of **Sicily** and the region of **Calabria** at the tip of the Italian “boot”. At its narrowest point it is only **a good 3 kilometres** wide. On the Sicilian side lies the city of **Messina**, and opposite on the mainland lies **Reggio Calabria**. In the north the strait borders the Tyrrhenian Sea, in the south the Ionian Sea.

There is still no bridge or tunnel. That is why **ferries** connect Sicily with the mainland. They carry people, cars, lorries and even whole **railway trains** across. The crossing does not take long. For many decades people have discussed building a large **bridge**, but the project is disputed and has been postponed again and again.

In the strait there are strong **currents** and whirlpools, because two seas with different tides meet. Even in ancient times the place was regarded as dangerous. In Greek legend the monsters **Scylla** and **Charybdis** lurked here, and the hero Odysseus had to sail past them. The area is also threatened by **earthquakes**: in 1908 a severe quake destroyed Messina and Reggio Calabria.

gewusst: The saying “between Scylla and Charybdis” means having to choose between two dangers, and comes from the legend about this strait.
On the ferries across the Strait of Messina, whole trains are split into sections and driven on board.

teile.einleitung: A steppe is a wide, flat grassland with almost no trees. Steppes exist on several continents. In each region they have a name of their own.
wichtigste: The steppe is wide grassland with almost no trees.
Too little rain falls in the steppe for trees.
In the steppes of Asia the winters are very cold and the summers hot.
In Mongolia many nomads move around with their herds and live in yurts.
In North America the steppe is called the prairie, in Argentina the pampas.
On many fertile steppe soils wheat is grown today.

abschnitte.text: In the **steppe** you see almost only **grass** all the way to the horizon. Trees hardly grow, because it **rains too little**. Grasses manage with less water than trees. In spring many colourful flowers often bloom in the steppe, and in summer the grass becomes dry and yellow. Steppes mostly lie far from the sea in the interior of the continents.

The great steppes of Asia lie very far from the sea. Otherwise the sea evens out the temperatures. That is why the **summers are hot** and the **winters very cold** there. Such a climate is called a **continental climate**. Often a strong wind blows across the flat land.

**Mongolia** lies in the interior of Asia and consists to a large extent of steppe. Many families are **nomads**: they move with their animals from pasture to pasture. They keep sheep, goats, cattle, camels and above all **horses**, on which they ride and herd their flocks. They live in **yurts**, round tents of wood and felt that can be taken down and taken along.

Steppes have a different name depending on the continent. In North America it is called the **prairie**. There huge herds of **bison** used to live. In Argentina it is called the **pampas**, and there many cattle graze today. In Eastern Europe, for example in Ukraine, and in Russia there are also large steppe areas.

Many steppe soils are very **fertile**. For centuries grasses grew and rotted, and in this way a thick, dark layer of soil formed, the **black earth**. Today grain such as **wheat** is grown on many former steppes. That is why some of these areas are also called the “granaries” of the world.

gewusst: A yurt can be put up and taken down again by a family in a few hours.
In Mongolia there are more horses than in many other countries, and even small children learn to ride there.

teile.einleitung: The Suez Canal is an artificial waterway in Egypt. It connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea. Thanks to it ships from Europe to Asia no longer have to sail all the way round Africa.
wichtigste: The Suez Canal lies in the north-east of Egypt.
It connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea.
It was opened in 1869, that is, in the 19th century.
It is about 190 kilometres long and needs no locks.
In March 2021 the container ship Ever Given blocked the canal.
Port Said lies at the northern end on the Mediterranean.

abschnitte.text: The **Suez Canal** lies in **Egypt** and is run by Egypt. It leads from the **Mediterranean** in the north to the **Red Sea** in the south. Before the canal, ships from Europe to Asia had to sail round the southern tip of **Africa**. The canal saves many thousands of kilometres and a lot of time. That is why it is one of the most important shipping lanes in the world.

The Suez Canal was opened in **1869**. The building was planned by the Frenchman **Ferdinand de Lesseps**. Thousands of workers dug it through the **desert** for over ten years. At the northern end the port city of **Port Said** arose during the building. There ships sail from the Mediterranean into the canal.

The canal is about **193 kilometres** long. Ships need about **eleven hours** for the passage. Unlike the Panama Canal it needs **no locks**, because the seas at both ends are almost the same height. On the right and left there is mostly flat desert, and from a distance it looks as if the ships are sailing through sand. On the way the canal passes through the **Great** and the **Little Bitter Lake**, where ships can pass each other.

In March **2021** the huge container ship **Ever Given** got stuck across the canal. For several days hundreds of ships could not pass through. Around the world goods were delivered late. With dredgers and tugs the ship was finally freed. This showed how important the canal is for world trade.

gewusst: A ship that cannot use the Suez Canal has to sail round the Cape of Good Hope and is on the way many days longer for it.
The Ever Given was about 400 metres long, almost as long as four football pitches end to end.

teile.einleitung: A lake is a larger body of standing water that is surrounded by land all round. Switzerland has very many lakes, from the large Lake Geneva to small mountain lakes. Most lakes contain fresh water and are important for nature, drinking water and leisure.
wichtigste: A lake is a body of standing water that is completely surrounded by land.
Most lakes have fresh water.
The largest lake in Switzerland is Lake Geneva.
At Lake Constance Switzerland, Germany and Austria meet.
The city of Lucerne lies on Lake Lucerne.
Many Swiss lakes were scooped out by glaciers of the Ice Age.
Lakes are a habitat for fish, birds and water plants.

abschnitte.text: A **lake** is a hollow in the land filled with water that is not directly connected to the sea. Usually streams or rivers flow into it, and a river flows out again. Almost all lakes have **fresh water**. There are also salt lakes, though, above all in dry areas, where a lot of water evaporates.

Many lakes in Switzerland formed in the last **Ice Age**. Huge glaciers carved out deep valleys, and when the ice melted, they filled with water. Other lakes form through rockfalls, in volcanic craters or when tectonic plates drift apart. A **reservoir** is made by humans with a dam, for example for producing electricity.

**Lake Geneva**, at about 580 square kilometres, is the largest lake in Switzerland, and part of it belongs to France. The largest lake lying entirely in Switzerland is Lake Neuchâtel. **Lake Constance** lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria. Lucerne lies on Lake Lucerne, Zurich on Lake Zurich and Lugano on Lake Lugano.

abschnitte.titel: Life in and by the lake
abschnitte.text: In lakes live fish such as whitefish, perch and pike. On the shore reeds and water lilies grow, in which waterbirds breed. In the past many Swiss lakes were heavily polluted by sewage and had too little oxygen. Thanks to **sewage treatment plants** and the ban on phosphate in detergents they are much cleaner again today.

Lakes supply **drinking water**; many cities such as Zurich or Geneva take part of their water from the lake. On Swiss lakes scheduled boats sail, including historic paddle steamers. In summer people swim, sail and paddle. Thousands of years ago people already built **pile dwellings** on lake shores, which are now part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

The largest lake on Earth is the **Caspian Sea** between Europe and Asia, which, despite its name, is a salt lake. The deepest lake is Lake Baikal in Siberia, at over 1,600 metres deep. It contains more fresh water than all the Great Lakes of North America put together. Lake Superior in North America is the largest freshwater lake by area.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water with very little salt, as in lakes, rivers and glaciers.
An artificial lake behind a dam.
A large stream of ice that moves slowly down the valley.
Houses on wooden stilts that people built on lake shores in the Stone Age.

gewusst: Lake Geneva is called Lac Léman in French-speaking Switzerland.
In winter some mountain lakes freeze so thickly that you can skate on them.
On Lake Constance the border between the countries has still not been exactly fixed today.

teile.einleitung: The Red Sea is a long, narrow sea between Africa and Asia. It is famous for its warm, very salty water and colourful coral reefs.
wichtigste: The Red Sea lies between Africa and Asia.
In the south it is connected with the Indian Ocean.
In the north lies the Sinai Peninsula with a famous mountain.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia, among others, lie on the Red Sea.
The water is warm and very salty.
Divers come because of the colourful coral reefs.
One explanation for the name is reddish algae in the water.

abschnitte.text: The Red Sea separates **Africa** from **Asia**. On the African side lie, for example, **Egypt**, Sudan and Eritrea. On the Arabian Peninsula lie **Saudi Arabia** and Yemen. In the south the sea is connected to the **Indian Ocean** by a strait. In the north the **Suez Canal** connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean.

In the north the Red Sea divides into two arms. Between them lies the **Sinai** Peninsula, which belongs to Egypt. There stands **Mount Sinai**. It is an important place in the Bible and in other religious traditions. The Red Sea lies in a **rift valley**, where Africa and the Arabian Peninsula are slowly moving apart.

The water in the Red Sea is **warm** all year round. It is also **very salty**, saltier than most other seas. The reason: in the hot desert air a lot of water evaporates, it hardly rains, and no large rivers flow into the sea. There are various explanations for the **name**. One of them is **reddish algae**, which sometimes colour the water.

The Red Sea is very popular with divers. It has **colourful coral reefs** with countless fish. In sea anemones live the orange and white striped **anemonefish**. The anemone’s poisonous stinging tentacles do not harm them and protect them from enemies. Popular holiday resorts in Egypt are, for example, **Hurghada** and Sharm el-Sheikh.

gewusst: The Red Sea becomes a tiny bit wider every year, because the continental plates are moving apart.
Many ships between Europe and Asia travel through the Suez Canal and the Red Sea.

teile.einleitung: Senegal is a country in West Africa on the Atlantic. The capital is Dakar, and the official language is French. In the country lies the westernmost point of the African mainland.
wichtigste: The capital of Senegal is Dakar.
The official language is French; in everyday life most people speak Wolof.
Near Dakar lies the westernmost point of the African mainland.
The small country of Gambia is almost completely surrounded by Senegal.
In the north Senegal borders Mauritania.
The baobab is a landmark of Senegal.

abschnitte.text: Senegal lies at the far west of Africa on the **Atlantic**. In the north lies **Mauritania**, in the east **Mali** and in the south **Guinea** and **Guinea-Bissau**. In the middle of the south of the country lies **Gambia**. It is a narrow strip along a river and almost completely enclosed by Senegal. Near Dakar lies the **Pointe des Almadies**, the westernmost point of the African mainland.

The capital **Dakar** lies on a peninsula on the Atlantic. It is also known through the **Dakar Rally**. This car race used to lead from Europe right across the Sahara to Dakar, but today it takes place elsewhere. The city of **Saint-Louis** lies on an island in the **Senegal River**. It was founded by the French and was for a long time the capital of **French West Africa**. Its old town is now a **UNESCO World Heritage** site.

Senegal used to be a **French colony** and became independent in **1960**. That is why **French** is the official language. In everyday life, however, most people speak **Wolof**, the language of the largest ethnic group. Almost everyone in the country understands it, even if they have a different mother tongue. The first president was **Léopold Sédar Senghor**, who was also a well-known poet.

A landmark of Senegal is the **baobab**. It has a very thick trunk and is shown on the country’s **coat of arms**. Not far from Dakar lies **Lake Retba**, also called the “Lac Rose”. Tiny algae in the very salty water often colour it **pink**. Salt is obtained at the lake.

Off Dakar lies the small island of **Gorée**. It recalls a dark time in history: over centuries many people were taken from the West African coast to America as **slaves**. Today Gorée is a **memorial site** and is also part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

gewusst: Lake Retba is so salty that you float in it as easily as in the Dead Sea.
Baobabs can live to be many hundreds of years old and store water in their trunks.

teile.einleitung: Saint Martin is a small island in the Caribbean. The special thing is that the island does not belong to a single state, but is divided between France and the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
wichtigste: Saint Martin lies in the Caribbean and belongs to the Lesser Antilles.
The north is called Saint-Martin and belongs to France.
The south is called Sint Maarten and belongs to the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
The division goes back to a treaty of 1648.
On the island it is warm all year round, and tourism is very important.

abschnitte.text: Saint Martin is only about as big as a small Swiss region around a lake. Even so, a **border** runs across the island. In the north lies the French part, **Saint-Martin**, in the south the Dutch part, **Sint Maarten**. You can cross the border without checks. Often there is only a monument or a sign at the roadside.

In the 17th century France and the Netherlands both wanted the island. In **1648** they agreed in a treaty to divide the island peacefully. A well-known **legend** tells that a Frenchman and a Dutchman walked round the island in opposite directions, and that the border was drawn where they met. That is only a story that people tell, though.

The French part is today an **overseas collectivity** of France in its own right. There people pay with the **euro**. The Dutch part, Sint Maarten, has been a country of its own within the **Kingdom of the Netherlands** since 2010. There a different currency applies, and the US dollar is also often used. The main towns are **Marigot** in the north and **Philipsburg** in the south.

abschnitte.titel: Holiday island with aeroplanes on the beach
abschnitte.text: Many people on the island work in **tourism**. Cruise ships call in, and guests come for the beaches and the warm sea. Famous is the beach **Maho Beach**: right behind it lies the runway of the airport, and the aeroplanes fly very low over the heads of the bathers. In the Caribbean there are also **hurricanes**. Hurricane Irma caused great damage on the island in 2017.

gewusst: Saint Martin is regarded as one of the smallest inhabited islands in the world that is divided between two states.
On a single small island you pay with euros in the north and with a different currency in the south.

teile.einleitung: Raw materials are substances from nature from which we make things or obtain energy. They include, for example, crude oil, copper, iron ore, wood, cotton or lithium. Without raw materials there would be no houses, cars, mobile phones or clothes.
wichtigste: Raw materials are unprocessed substances from nature that serve as the starting material.
Aluminium is obtained mainly from the ore bauxite.
For years China has produced the largest part of the world’s rare earths.
The largest part of the cobalt in 2025 came from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Argentina, Bolivia and Chile form the so-called lithium triangle.
The resource curse describes how countries rich in raw materials often develop badly.
Geneva and Zug are regarded as important centres of international commodity trading.

abschnitte.text: A **raw material** is a substance from nature that has not yet been processed. A distinction is made between **mineral** raw materials such as ores, salt and sand, **energy raw materials** such as crude oil, natural gas and coal, and **renewable** raw materials such as wood, cotton or grain. In factories, raw materials are turned into materials and products. For example, aluminium is made from bauxite, and you need it for drinks cans and bicycles.

abschnitte.titel: Raw materials in our everyday lives
abschnitte.text: In a mobile phone there are dozens of different raw materials, such as copper, gold, cobalt and **rare earths**. For the batteries of electric cars you need lithium, cobalt and nickel. Lithium is obtained mainly in Australia and in the **lithium triangle** in South America, often from salt lakes. For wind turbines and electric motors you need magnets made of rare earths, which come largely from China.

Some raw materials such as crude oil are **not renewable** and will run out at some point. You can calculate how long the known reserves will last: with reserves of 1,200 billion barrels and production of 30 billion barrels a year it would be 40 years. Such figures change, however, because new deposits are discovered and consumption changes. A barrel is a drum holding about 159 litres.

You might think that countries with many raw materials are especially rich. Often, though, the opposite is the case, which is called the **resource curse**. When a country lives almost only from one raw material, often only a few people benefit, and corruption or conflicts arise. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, children also work in some cobalt mines under dangerous conditions.

Switzerland itself has hardly any natural resources, apart from gravel, salt, wood and a lot of water. Even so, it is an important place for **commodity trading**: in Geneva and Zug large trading firms have their headquarters, buying and selling oil, metals and grain from all over the world. The raw materials themselves mostly do not even come to Switzerland. In 2020 Switzerland voted on the Responsible Business Initiative, which demanded stricter liability for such firms, and rejected it because it failed to win a majority of the cantons.

Many raw materials can be reused. In Switzerland aluminium cans, glass, paper and old electrical appliances are collected and **recycled**. From old mobile phones you can recover gold, silver and copper. Because so many raw materials are contained in cities and waste, people also speak of “urban mining”, mining in the city.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rock from which metals can be obtained.
A group of metals that are needed for magnets, screens and electronics.
When a country stays poor or runs into problems despite many raw materials.
Reusing waste in order to obtain new raw materials from it.
A unit of measurement for oil, a drum holding about 159 litres.

gewusst: The rare earths are not really so rare, but they are difficult to mine.
The Swiss salt works obtain salt from deposits deep underground, for example near Rheinfelden and Bex.
Recycling aluminium needs only a small part of the energy that is needed for new aluminium.

teile.einleitung: Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish scientist. In 1896 he was one of the first to calculate that more carbon dioxide in the air warms the Earth. In doing so he laid an important foundation for climate research.
wichtigste: Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist and physicist.
In 1896 he calculated that more CO2 in the air warms the Earth.
He is one of the founders of physical chemistry.
In 1903 he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
His calculations are seen as an early foundation of research into the greenhouse effect.

abschnitte.text: **Svante Arrhenius** lived from **1859 to 1927** and came from Sweden. He worked on chemistry, physics and the climate of the Earth. He became well known for his research into how substances split into electrically charged particles in water. He is regarded as one of the founders of **physical chemistry**. For this he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in **1903**, the first Swede to do so.

In **1896** Arrhenius asked an important question: how much would the Earth warm up if there were more **carbon dioxide** (CO2) in the air? He did the sums by hand for many months. His result: more CO2 holds back more heat, so the Earth gets warmer. Today this process is called the **greenhouse effect**. At the time Arrhenius was thinking mainly of possible causes of the ice ages.

In his day Arrhenius believed that people would produce more CO2 only very slowly, for example by burning coal. Today it happens much faster. His basic idea has nevertheless been confirmed. Arrhenius is therefore seen as one of the pioneers of **climate research**. Modern climate models are far more precise, but they are built on the same laws of physics.

gewusst: Arrhenius even thought a slight warming would be a good thing, because it could make cold countries such as Sweden milder.
A crater on the Moon is named after Arrhenius.

teile.einleitung: A deciduous summer-green forest bears leaves in summer and is bare in winter. Such forests grow in areas with four seasons, including large parts of Switzerland. Over the course of the year the forest changes greatly.
wichtigste: Deciduous summer-green forests grow in a temperate climate with four seasons.
The trees shed their leaves in autumn so that they do not dry out in winter.
The beech is the most common broadleaf tree in Switzerland.
Early bloomers such as the wood anemone use the light before the trees have leaves.
A forest has layers: moss, herb, shrub and tree layers.
Earthworms, fungi and bacteria turn fallen leaves into humus.

abschnitte.text: Deciduous summer-green forests grow where there are warm summers, cool winters and rain in all seasons. This is called a **temperate climate**. A large part of **Central Europe** belongs to it, including the Swiss Plateau. In spring the trees put out new leaves, and in summer the forest is dense and shady. In autumn the leaves change colour and fall, and in winter the trees are bare.

In winter the ground is often frozen. The roots can then hardly take up any **water**. But water would keep evaporating through the leaves. That is why the tree sheds its leaves, otherwise it would dry out. Beforehand it breaks down the green pigment **chlorophyll** and stores valuable substances from it. Then the **yellow and orange pigments** become visible, which were already in the leaf before.

In early spring the trees still have no leaves. Then a lot of **light** reaches the forest floor. Plants such as the **wood anemone**, wild garlic or lesser celandine use this short time. They are called **early bloomers**. They store their reserves in bulbs, tubers or rootstocks. As soon as the leaf canopy has closed, it becomes shady on the ground.

A deciduous forest is built like a house with storeys. At the very bottom lies the **moss layer**. Above it follows the **herb layer** with grasses, ferns and flowers. Then comes the **shrub layer** with hazel bushes and young trees. At the very top is the **tree layer**. In Switzerland the **beech** is the most common broadleaf tree, and only the spruce as a conifer is more common still. Oaks, maples and ash trees also grow in the deciduous forest.

Every year a lot of leaves fall to the ground. **Earthworms** pull leaves into the soil, eat them and pass them out again as nutrient-rich crumbs. Together with **fungi** and **bacteria**, **humus** is formed in this way. Under deciduous forests the fertile **brown earth** often forms. It is a common soil on the Swiss Plateau.

gewusst: The yellow colour of autumn leaves is already in the leaf in summer, it is only hidden by the green.
Without earthworms, fungi and bacteria the forest would sink under a mountain of old leaves.

teile.einleitung: The soya bean is a plant from the legume family, related to peas and beans. It comes from East Asia and is today one of the most important crops in the world, because its beans contain a great deal of protein and oil.
wichtigste: The soya bean is a legume and originally comes from China.
Its beans contain a lot of protein and oil.
Tofu, soya drink, soy sauce and cooking oil are made from soya.
Most of the harvest is used as animal feed.
Brazil is the largest soya producer in the world (as of 2024).
Rainforest and savannas were cleared for new soya fields.

abschnitte.text: The **soya bean** belongs to the **legumes**, like peas, lentils and garden beans. The beans grow in small, hairy **pods**. In **China** soya has been grown for thousands of years. From there the plant spread to Japan, Korea and later all over the world.

Soya beans contain especially a lot of **protein** and **oil**. That is why they are very valuable. **Soya oil** is pressed out of the beans. What is left is the protein-rich **soya meal**. It is used mainly as feed for pigs, chickens and cattle. Only a small part of the harvest is eaten directly by people.

In Asian cooking soya is very important. **Tofu**, **soya drink** and **soy sauce** are made from soya beans. **Edamame**, young green soya beans, are also gladly eaten as a snack. Many vegetarian products such as meat substitutes contain soya. Because soya supplies a lot of protein, it is an important source of food for people who do not eat meat.

The largest soya producers are **Brazil**, the **USA** and **Argentina**. Brazil has overtaken the USA and is the largest producer in the world (as of 2024). A large part of the harvest is exported as **animal feed**. For new fields **rainforest** and **savannas** were cleared. That is why many countries, Switzerland among them, pay attention to soya from responsible farming. In Switzerland soya is also grown at home, but only in small amounts.

On the roots of the soya plant live **nodule bacteria**. They can take **nitrogen** from the air and make it usable for the plant. Nitrogen is an important nutrient for growing. That is why soya needs little nitrogen fertiliser. This is an advantage that all legumes have.

gewusst: Edamame are young soya beans that you boil in the pod and then squeeze out.
With the help of bacteria, soya plants get fertiliser straight from the air.

teile.einleitung: With daylight saving time we put the clocks forward one hour in spring and back again in autumn. This way it stays light longer in the evening. In Switzerland daylight saving time has been used every year since 1981.
wichtigste: Daylight saving time begins on the last Sunday in March.
Then the clock is put forward from 2 o’clock to 3 o’clock.
It ends on the last Sunday in October, when the day has 25 hours.
Switzerland introduced daylight saving time in 1981.
In 1978 the Swiss electorate narrowly rejected a time law.
Originally daylight saving time was meant above all to save energy.

abschnitte.text: Daylight saving time begins in the night to the **last Sunday in March**. At 2 o’clock the clock jumps straight to **3 o’clock**. This hour is lost, and the day has only 23 hours. On the **last Sunday in October** daylight saving time ends. Then the clock is put back from 3 o’clock to 2 o’clock. The hour from 2 to 3 o’clock is experienced twice, so the day has **25 hours**.

abschnitte.titel: Why is there daylight saving time?
abschnitte.text: Originally people wanted to **save energy** with daylight saving time. When it is light for longer in the evening, you need less artificial light. That is why it was introduced mainly in times of crisis. One of the first states to introduce daylight saving time was the **German Empire**, together with Austria-Hungary, on 30 April 1916, during the First World War. Other countries soon followed.

Already during the Second World War Switzerland put the clocks forward in summer in **1941 and 1942** to save energy. After that it did without for a long time. On **28 May 1978** the people voted on a **time law** that would have made daylight saving time possible. It was narrowly rejected, with only 47.9 per cent in favour. When the neighbouring countries changed over, Switzerland became a “time island” for a short while. Since **1981** daylight saving time has applied in Switzerland every year too.

Switzerland follows the rules of the **European Union**. Since 1996 daylight saving time has ended everywhere on the last Sunday in October. Before that it already ended at the end of September. Because the dates always fall on a Sunday, the exact day changes every year. In this way the neighbouring countries and Switzerland always have the same time.

The clock change is disputed. Some people feel tired after the change, others enjoy the long, light evenings. In 2018 the **European Commission** ran an online survey with about 4.6 million participants. About **84 per cent** wanted to abolish the clock change. So far this has not been carried out, because the countries do not agree which time should then apply.

gewusst: On the day daylight saving time ends, the time 2:30 occurs twice.
In 1980 Switzerland was a “time island”, because daylight saving time already applied all around.

teile.einleitung: In an earthquake different waves spread through the Earth. The S-wave is one of them. It has helped researchers to find out how the inside of the Earth is built.
wichtigste: The S-wave is a transverse wave or shear wave.
It is about 60 per cent as fast as the P-wave in the same rock.
S-waves cannot spread through liquids.
From this it was concluded that the outer core of the Earth is liquid.
In 1914 Beno Gutenberg determined the boundary of the core at a depth of about 2,900 km.
S-waves usually do more damage to buildings than P-waves.

abschnitte.text: The **S** stands for **secondary**, that is, the second, because S-waves arrive after the P-waves. The S-wave is a **transverse wave** or **shear wave**. This means: the rock swings **across** the direction in which the wave spreads. You can imagine it like a rope that you shake up and down. In the **P-wave**, by contrast, the rock is squeezed together and stretched in the direction of travel.

The S-wave is about **60 per cent** as fast as the P-wave in the same rock. That is why it always arrives **later** at a measuring station. From the time difference between the P-wave and the S-wave, experts can calculate how far away the **earthquake** was. After the S-wave come the **surface waves**. They are called **Love waves** and **Rayleigh waves**.

S-waves can spread only through **solid** materials, not through liquids. Researchers noticed that beyond a distance of about **103 degrees** from the earthquake no direct S-waves arrive. From this they concluded that the **outer core is liquid**. The researcher **Beno Gutenberg** determined in **1914** the boundary between the mantle and the core at a depth of about **2,900 km**.

S-waves usually cause **more damage** to buildings than P-waves. They have larger **amplitudes**, that is, stronger deflections, and shake houses **sideways** back and forth. Many buildings are less well prepared for this. That is why in Switzerland there are building regulations for **earthquake-proof construction**. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich measures all the earthquakes in the country.

gewusst: Some early warning systems use the faster P-wave to warn of the stronger S-wave.
The boundary between the mantle and the core is also called the Gutenberg discontinuity, after its discoverer.

teile.einleitung: A slum is a poor residential district in a city where people live in a small space in simple huts. Often clean water, sewers and electricity are missing. Worldwide about a billion people live in such settlements.
wichtigste: A slum is a residential area with very simple shelters and little infrastructure.
Slums often arise without permission on the edge of a city or on steep slopes.
In Brazil such districts are called favelas, in Turkey gecekondu.
Kibera in Nairobi and Dharavi in Mumbai are among the largest slums.
According to the UN, about a billion people live in slums.
UN-Habitat is the UN organisation for cities and housing.

abschnitte.text: A **slum** is a residential area with very simple shelters, often made of corrugated iron, wood or plastic. The houses stand close together. Many slums arise without permission and without planning. That is why people also speak of **informal settlements**. The residents usually do not own the land and can be driven out at any time.

Many people move from the countryside to the city because they look for work and a better life there. This is called **rural flight**. But cities grow faster than new homes are built. Someone with little money therefore builds a hut of their own on the edge of the city. This is how slums often grow very quickly.

In Brazil the poor districts are called **favelas**. In Rio de Janeiro many lie on steep hills. In South Africa there are the **townships**. They were laid out in the time of **apartheid**, when black people had to live separately on the edge of the city. The best known is **Soweto**. **Kibera** in Nairobi, the capital of Kenya, and **Dharavi** in Mumbai, India, are among the largest slums in the world. In Dharavi there are many small workshops, for example for recycling, pottery and leather.

In slums **sewers**, clean **drinking water** and a safe supply of electricity are often missing. Many families share one toilet or one tap. This makes illnesses spread more easily. Even so, slums also have schools, shops and a lot of community spirit. Many people work hard, often without a fixed contract.

The UN programme **UN-Habitat** works for better housing conditions and sustainable cities. It is based in Nairobi. According to the UN, about **a billion people** live in slums and informal settlements. Some cities build water pipes and roads in existing slums instead of tearing them down. It is also important that people get a secure right to their home.

gewusst: Gecekondu means “built overnight” in Turkish.
About one in every seven or eight people in the world lives in a slum or an informal settlement.

teile.einleitung: The taiga is a huge coniferous forest in the north of the Earth. It stretches like a broad belt through Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska.
wichtigste: The taiga is a coniferous forest in the far north.
Mainly spruce, pine and larch grow there.
Most of it lies in Russia, and there is a lot of taiga in Canada too.
The winters are long and very cold, and the summers are short.
North of the taiga lies the tundra.
Elk, brown bears, wolves and lynx live in the taiga.

abschnitte.text: The taiga is a **coniferous forest** in the north of Europe, Asia and North America. It is also called the **boreal forest**, meaning the forest of the north. It is the largest forest area on land. Most of it lies in **Russia**, especially in Siberia. There is also a lot of taiga in **Canada**, in Alaska and in Scandinavia.

The **winters** in the taiga are **long and very cold**, often far below minus 20 degrees. The summers are short but can get quite warm. In parts of Siberia the ground deep down is frozen all year round, which is called **permafrost**. There are many bogs, lakes and rivers. **North** of the taiga it becomes too cold for trees, and the **tundra** begins.

Mainly **spruce**, **pine**, **fir** and **larch** grow in the taiga. Their needles have a waxy coating that protects them from cold and drying out. The **larch** is special: it loses its needles in autumn and so survives the icy winters of Siberia. Birch trees grow there too. Larches are also known in Switzerland, for example in the Engadin.

The large **elk** with its broad antlers lives in the taiga. There are also **brown bears**, **wolves**, **lynx** and the wolverine. In the east of Russia even the **Siberian tiger** lives. Many birds fly south in autumn. Some animals spend the winter resting, like the brown bear.

gewusst: The taiga stores huge amounts of carbon in its trees and soils and is therefore important for the climate.
Forest fires are a natural part of the taiga: some pines only open their cones after a fire.

teile.einleitung: The Taklamakan is a huge sand desert in the north-west of China. It is surrounded by high mountains and used to be considered dangerous for travellers.
wichtigste: The Taklamakan lies in China, in the region of Xinjiang.
It fills most of the Tarim Basin.
About 85 per cent of the desert is covered by shifting dunes.
The Tian Shan lies to the north and the Kunlun Shan to the south.
The Silk Road ran along the edge of the desert.
Well-preserved mummies were found in the dry sand.

abschnitte.text: The Taklamakan lies in the north-west of **China** in the region of **Xinjiang**. It is about eight times the size of Switzerland and is one of the largest **sand deserts** in the world. About **85 per cent** of it is covered by **shifting dunes**, which the wind slowly pushes along. In summer it is hot, and in winter it is very cold. Sandstorms often rage.

The desert fills most of the **Tarim Basin**. All around stand high mountains: the **Tian Shan** to the north, the **Kunlun Shan** to the south and the Pamir to the west. The mountains keep the rain away, which is why it is so dry. The **Tarim** flows along the northern edge. It gets its water from the glaciers and in the end seeps away into the sand.

The old **Silk Road** ran along the edge of the Taklamakan. The caravans avoided the desert itself and travelled to the north and south, from **oasis to oasis**. Well-known oasis towns are **Kashgar** and Hotan. The name “Taklamakan” is often interpreted as “**Whoever goes in does not come out**”. This interpretation is not certain linguistically, but it shows how feared the desert was.

In the dry sand at the edge of the desert, researchers found **well-preserved mummies**. These **Tarim mummies** are several thousand years old. The dry air and the salty soil preserved them naturally. The remains of old towns and monasteries also lie under the sand.

gewusst: In 1895 the Swedish explorer Sven Hedin got into great trouble in the Taklamakan when his water ran out.
Today a road runs straight across the desert, protected from the sand by planted vegetation.

teile.einleitung: A beach is the flat edge between land and water. By the sea or a lake there is sand, gravel or stones there. Many people like to spend their holidays on the beach.
wichtigste: Sand mostly consists of tiny grains of rock, often quartz.
Wet sand is good for building sandcastles.
On the beach you often find shells.
A beach of round stones is called a shingle beach.
Sun cream and a hat protect against sunburn.

abschnitte.text: Sand consists of **tiny grains of rock**. The **waves** rub stones against one another over a very long time until they are quite small. Mostly the grains consist of the mineral **quartz**. But there are also beaches with black sand from volcanic rock or with light sand from ground-up shells and corals. If there are round stones on the beach instead of sand, it is called a **shingle beach**. The waves have ground the stones round.

On the beach you often find **shells** and snail shells. Mussels and snails live in the sea, and their empty shells are washed ashore by the waves. Sometimes you also find starfish, seaweed or smooth driftwood. Sadly rubbish such as plastic is washed up too, so many people help to clean up beaches.

With **wet sand** you can build great **sandcastles**. The water between the grains makes them stick together, so towers and walls hold. Dry sand, by contrast, trickles apart. In Switzerland too there are beaches, for example on lakes such as Lake Geneva or Lake Neuchâtel, where children swim and play in summer.

On the beach the **Sun** is especially strong, because water and sand throw the light back. That is why you protect yourself against **sunburn** with **sun cream**, a sun hat, a T-shirt and sunglasses. Over midday it is best to look for shade. In the water the rule is: only swim where it is safe, and pay attention to warning flags.

gewusst: A single grain of sand can be many thousands of years old.
There are beaches with black, pink or even greenish sand.

teile.einleitung: The Ruhr region in Germany was for a long time the largest industrial area in Europe. Coal and steel shaped the region until the last German hard coal mine was closed in 2018.
wichtigste: The Ruhr region lies in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
It is named after the River Ruhr.
Large cities are Essen, Dortmund, Duisburg and Bochum.
For many decades coal mining and the steel industry shaped the region.
In 2018 the last German hard coal mine was closed here.
The Zollverein colliery in Essen is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

abschnitte.text: The **Ruhr region** lies in the west of Germany in the state of **North Rhine-Westphalia**. It is named after the River **Ruhr**, which flows into the Rhine. Here many large cities lie close together, for example **Essen**, **Dortmund**, **Duisburg**, **Bochum** and Gelsenkirchen. It is one of the largest urban areas in Europe. Several million people live there.

In the 19th century people began to mine **hard coal** on a large scale in the Ruhr region. A mine is called a **Zeche** there. The coal was used to fire blast furnaces in which **steel** was made. Many people moved to the region as workers. Coal and steel made the Ruhr region the most important **industrial area** in Germany.

Later coal from other countries became cheaper, and many mines closed. Steelworks shut down too. In **2018** the last German **hard coal mine** was closed, the **Prosper-Haniel** mine in Bottrop.
